Adams County by the numbers

Where is Adams County and which offices handle its property tax?

Quincy anchors Adams County, the state's westernmost county, which touches Missouri along its western edge. Settlers organized it in 1825 from Pike County, and it covers 871 square miles. A sale touches four offices: the collector, the Supervisor of Assessments, a township assessor and the Board of Review.

The collector, who is also the county treasurer, sends and takes in tax payments at 507 Vermont St, Suite G12, in Quincy (217-277-2245). The Supervisor of Assessments runs exemptions and equalization, and the Board of Review hears assessment complaints in the Adams County Courthouse. Villages such as Camp Point, Mendon, Payson, Golden, Liberty and Clayton sit inside the county's 23 townships, so a house outside Quincy is usually assessed by a township assessor rather than a city office.

  • Roads: I-172, US 24 and US 36 run through Quincy, with Illinois routes 57, 61, 94, 96, 104 and 110 across the county.
  • Population: the Census Bureau puts 2025 at 64,267, a loss of about 1,500 people since the 2020 count of 65,737.
  • Housing: 72.1% of households own, the middle owned home is worth $162,600, and renters typically pay $828.
  • Households earn a median of $66,220, and nearly one resident in four (22.8%) is 65 or over.

How does the Adams County tax cycle work for someone selling?

Bills here trail the assessment by a year. The 2025 assessment was paid during 2026, and it reflected the home's value and exemptions on January 1, 2025. Someone who closes mid-year therefore still owes for a stretch the county has not yet billed.

The collector's guide for new owners says whoever is owner of record once a deed is recorded answers for later bills. Bills go out in late spring. The first installment falls around June 1, or 30 days after mailing if that is later, and the second around September 1. A buyer may pay both halves at once or split them into two equal payments.

Adams County collection calendar for taxes payable in 2026 (source: Adams County Treasurer)
StepDate on the county calendar
Real estate bills mailedMay 22 (tentative)
First installment dueJuly 2 (tentative)
Second installment dueSeptember 1
$10 mail and publication fee addedOctober 1
Last day to pay before the saleOctober 23
Annual tax saleOctober 26

All of those 2026 dates have passed. Ask the collector for the calendar covering the tax year you are closing in, since the county marks several dates as tentative.

What does the Adams County collector require for late payments?

For tax paid after September 30, the collector wants a cashier's check, money order, cash or a card, and personal, business and e-checks are turned away. The statute sets late interest at 1 1/2% per month or fraction of a month, and mail postmarked by the due date counts as on time (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

The county calendar lists a $10 mail and publication fee on October 1, a published list of delinquent parcels, and a last day for card payments before the sale. October 22 was marked as judgment day. A seller with unpaid tax should clear it before the sale, because a parcel sold at tax sale complicates title.

  • Before a listing, ask the collector at 217-277-2245 whether any installment is open.
  • Have the title agent run a tax search so any payoff appears on the settlement statement.
  • Keep the postmarked envelope or bank confirmation if you pay close to a due date.

How is a house in Adams County assessed, and how do I appeal?

The county assessment office states that a home outside Cook County is assessed at 33 1/3 percent of market value. To check your own number, divide the assessed value by what you think the home would sell for, then compare that ratio with similar homes in your area.

Complaints go to the Board of Review in writing. For counties under 150,000 residents the filing date is August 10, a date that can move if the Supervisor of Assessments missed a required publishing date. The Board of Review generally sits Monday through Thursday, 8:30 to 11:30 a.m., between July 10 and October 7. It reviews the written complaint, sends a tentative decision, and you may then ask for a hearing, with or without an attorney.

The Board does not change a tax bill. It changes the assessment the bill is built on, and it publishes a list of changes in a county newspaper after it adjourns. If the Board's answer is unsatisfactory, you may appeal in writing to the State Property Tax Appeal Board.

  • Strong grounds: a value estimate above what the home would sell for, wrong lot or building measurements, or an assessment above those of similar neighbors.
  • Helpful evidence: your deed or transfer declaration, a current appraisal, nearby comparable sales with photos, and the property record card.
  • An assessment complaint filed late cannot fix a bill that has already gone out.

Which exemptions can an Adams County homeowner claim?

The Supervisor of Assessments lists the following relief on the county tax relief page. Dollar figures are as that page prints them and reduce equalized assessed value, not the bill directly.

  • General homestead: the growth in equalized value since 1977, to a ceiling of $6,000, where the owner lives in the house.
  • Senior citizens: $5,000 off equalized value, available at 65.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income capped at $75,000, with a renewal each year.
  • Homestead improvement: value from new construction, at most $75,000 a year, running four years after the work is finished and occupied.
  • Returning veterans: $5,000 for two consecutive years.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000, applied for every year.
  • Disabled veterans standard exemption: $2,500 for a rating from 30% up to 50%, $5,000 from 50% up to 70%, and total relief from 70%.

Most of these require the owner to live in the home, so a buyer applies in their own name after taking title.

What if I have deferred my taxes under the senior program?

This matters for a sale. Qualified owners can postpone up to $7,500 of tax a year through the state's Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program. The treasurer's package puts simple interest at 3 percent from tax year 2023 onward and says the county records a lien on the house. Applicants need to be 65 by June 1, with household income at or below $65,000 and three years of living in the home or a similar qualifying one.

The package adds that a sale or transfer cannot legally close and record until the deferred amounts are paid, and the balance comes due 90 days after a sale. Filing is in person at the treasurer's office from January 1 through March 1. If you hold a deferral, get a payoff figure from the treasurer early and have it settled out of your proceeds.

How do I pay Adams County property tax?

You can pay by several routes, and each has its own rule. The collector's office is inside the North 5th Street entrance of the courthouse, staffed on weekdays from half past eight until half past four.

  • Online by e-check or card; the page prints $1.50 per e-check and 2.25% of the payment for cards ($2.00 minimum).
  • A drop box outside the North 5th Street entrance that is available around the clock (no cash).
  • Mail to Adams County Collector, 507 Vermont St STE G12, Quincy, IL 62301-2998, where the postmark date counts.
  • Participating banks, for real estate tax only and never after the due date.
  • Bank bill pay, using the full parcel number without dashes as the account.

Tax records and duplicate bills are available online at no charge through the county's tax lookup.

How are taxes and splits handled when the house sells?

The collector's guide says the closing statement may include a credit from the seller for estimated unbilled and unpaid tax, and that the exact figure is unknown until bills are created. In most cases the new owner receives the next bill and pays the seller's share. Give the buyer or the title company a mailing address, since the county uses one address for bills, assessment notices and legal notices.

The office pauses deed and address updates for one to two weeks in mid-April while bills are produced. Splits and combined parcels recorded after August 10 do not take effect until January of the next tax year, and the original owner still gets the original bill. Decide in the contract who pays it.

More questions about Adams County, IL Property Tax Guide

When are Adams County property tax installments due?

They fall around June 1 (or 30 days after mailing if later) and around September 1. For taxes payable in 2026 the county calendar showed July 2 as tentative and September 1 as firm. The date printed on your bill is the one that counts.

What if my Quincy-area tax bill never arrives?

Phone the collector at 217-277-2245. The county calendar asks owners without a bill to call in mid-June, and tax records and duplicate bills are online at no charge.

Can I appeal my Adams County assessment after the August 10 date?

Not normally. For counties under 150,000 residents the Board of Review filing date is August 10, though the Board's page says it can be extended when publishing dates were missed. Ask the Supervisor of Assessments which date applies to your township.

Will the senior deferral stop me from selling a house in Adams County?

It will not stop a sale, but it must be paid first. The treasurer's package says no transfer may be closed and recorded until deferred taxes and interest are paid, so request a payoff early.

Does the Board of Review lower my tax bill directly in Adams County?

No. The Board of Review changes the assessment, and the bill is then built from the new value. The county's own page says the Board has no authority to change a tax bill itself.

Boone County by the numbers

What should a Boone County seller know about the county itself?

Boone County sits in far northern Illinois along the Wisconsin line and belongs to the Rockford metro area. The county was formed from Winnebago County on March 3, 1836, and bears Daniel Boone's name. Belvidere serves as both seat and largest city. The county covers about 282 square miles in nine townships: Belvidere, Bonus, Boone, Caledonia, Flora, Leroy, Manchester, Poplar Grove and Spring.

Interstate 90, US 20 and Illinois routes 76 and 173 carry most traffic. Besides Belvidere, the incorporated places include Poplar Grove, Cherry Valley, Capron, Caledonia and Timberlane, plus the Candlewick Lake community. School districts that reach into the county are Belvidere 100, Harvard 50, Hiawatha 426, North Boone 200 and Rockford 205, so your bill names whichever district serves your street. The southern townships lie on the broad floodplains of the Kishwaukee River and its tributaries, while the northern townships have higher ground and more surface relief. Winters are cold: Belvidere averages an 11 degree January low and an 85 degree July high.

  • The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 53,568 people, a gain of two tenths of a percent over 2020.
  • Four in five households own: the ownership rate is 81.8%, and the typical owned home is valued at $216,900.
  • Renters pay a median of $1,041 a month, while the median household earns $84,571.
  • Workers travel 26.6 minutes on average to their jobs, and 2,308 residents are veterans.

Which Boone County offices send and collect the bill?

Three offices share the work. The Treasurer mails and collects bills from the Boone County Administration Campus, 1212 Logan Avenue, Suite 104, Belvidere, and can be reached at 815-544-2666. The Assessment Office (Supervisor of Assessments) answers exemption and assessment questions at 815-544-2958. The County Clerk lists real property and handles redemption after a tax sale.

The county's own overview describes a six-step cycle: the Clerk lists the property, the township assessor values it as of January 1, the county office equalizes townships to one-third of market value, the Board of Review hears complaints, the Clerk calculates rates, and the Treasurer bills and collects. A buyer or seller who understands that order knows which window is still open.

When is Boone County property tax due, and how can I pay it?

The treasurer's FAQ says bills normally go out in late April, with half due June 1 and half due September 1. You may settle the whole amount by June 1 if you prefer. State law makes no allowance for partial payments.

  • At nearly any bank in the county, bringing the whole bill if you want it stamped as proof.
  • By mail, with a check made out to the Boone County Treasurer and a postmark no later than the due date.
  • Through your bank's bill-pay service, using the property number as the vendor account number.
  • Online by card or e-check, where a convenience fee of up to 2.5% is added to the total.
  • At the Logan Avenue office, paying with cash, a check or a money order, Monday through Friday from 8:30 until 5:00.

The treasurer does not take cards in the office or by phone. If a mortgage escrow pays your tax, check the payment status on the treasurer's website shortly before the due date and call the lender if it is still open.

How does a Boone County assessment appeal work?

A written complaint to the Boone County Board of Review is due 30 days after the assessment changes are published, or September 10 if that comes later. The Assessment Office provides the complaint forms and the staff for the Board of Review.

A value complaint must include your own opinion of what the property was worth on January 1 of the assessment year, backed by evidence. The county lists a closing statement for a recent purchase, at least three sales of comparable properties within one year of the assessment date, a recent appraisal, and income and expense statements for investment property. A complaint of unequal treatment needs the address, parcel number and assessed value of three or more comparison properties.

The Board mails a tentative notice. An owner who disagrees calls the Assessment Office within the time on that notice to book a hearing. Once the final notice arrives, the owner has 30 days to take the case to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board in Springfield, and Circuit Court review remains available after that. Mark the 30-day window on your calendar as soon as the assessment list appears in the newspaper.

What exemptions and limits reduce a Boone County tax bill?

The Assessment Office administers the homestead exemptions and the preferential assessments. As that office prints them:

  • General homestead: a reduction equal to the rise in equalized value since 1977, capped at $6,000, for a home the owner lives in.
  • Senior citizens: a $5,000 reduction for owners aged 65 and over; the first application (form PTAX-324) goes to the county assessment officer.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income below $75,000 for 2025, with form PTAX-340 filed each year.
  • Homestead improvement: value added by new work, to a yearly maximum of $75,000, lasting four years.
  • Disabled persons: a $2,000 reduction for the primary residence.
  • Veterans with service-connected disabilities: $2,500 for a 30% to 49% rating, $5,000 for 50% to 69%, and the first $250,000 of value at 70% or more.

The county also explains that the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law holds each taxing district's yearly increase to the lesser of 5 percent or inflation, plus new construction. Its page adds that this is not a cap on any single bill, because assessments and exemptions can still move an individual total.

What happens if a Boone County tax bill goes unpaid?

The treasurer's page lays out the sequence below, measured from the second installment date. It describes the figures as approximate, because state statute controls them.

Unpaid-tax timeline in Boone County (source: Boone County Treasurer)
WhenWhat happens
One day after the deadlineA 1.5% penalty attaches, then 1.5% more each month
About two weeks afterCertified delinquency notice and a $10.00 fee
About one month afterList of delinquent parcels printed in a local newspaper
About two months afterTax sale; investors pay the tax plus about $44.00 in fees
Within 4 1/2 months of sale"Take notice" mailed by the County Clerk
About 2 1/2 years after saleRedemption ends and the buyer may petition for a tax deed

The redemption rate is set at the sale and can reach 18% per six months. After a sale, redemption is made through the County Clerk with cash, cashier's check or money order, and no installment plan is allowed. Title does not change at the sale itself.

Who pays the Boone County tax bill when the house sells?

According to the treasurer, sellers usually give the buyer a credit at closing for tax that has built up, and the buyer then answers for the next bill. Because an unpaid bill becomes a lien against the parcel, a new owner should verify that the earlier tax was settled.

Because tax is billed in arrears, a house sold in the fall still has an unbilled bill to come. Get the credit in writing, go over each line of the settlement statement, and request a payment-status check on the parcel before you sign.

More questions about Boone County, IL Property Tax Guide

How long do Belvidere-area owners have to contest a value?

Yes. The complaint window runs 30 days from publication of the changes, or to September 10 when that is later. Once the Board rules, a further 30 days applies for an appeal to the state Property Tax Appeal Board.

Can the tax be split into two payments in Boone County?

Yes, in the two installments due June 1 and September 1. The treasurer notes that partial payments are not allowed, so each installment has to be paid whole.

Is there a surcharge for paying Boone County tax by card?

Online card or e-check payments carry convenience fees of up to 2.5%, shown at checkout. The treasurer's office cannot accept cards in person or by phone.

What role does the County Clerk play after a Boone County tax sale?

The Clerk collects redemption money in certified funds and mails the tax buyer's take-notice letter within about 4 1/2 months of the sale. Payment plans are not accepted.

How do I reach the Boone County Assessment Office?

Call 815-544-2958 for questions about assessments, exemptions and address changes. The Treasurer, which handles bills and payments, is at 1212 Logan Avenue, Suite 104, Belvidere, at 815-544-2666.

What kind of county is Bureau County for a home seller?

Bureau County is a largely rural county in north-central Illinois, created from Putnam County in 1837 and named for the Bureau brothers, French Canadian traders who ran a post near Big Bureau Creek and the Illinois River. Princeton holds the courthouse and is also the biggest city. The county covers 874 square miles, of which 869 are land, and it belongs to the Ottawa micropolitan area. Part of the Hennepin Canal Parkway State Park lies inside it.

With about 38 people per square mile and 55% of residents living in rural areas in the 2020 census, this market looks different from the suburbs. Winters bring a January low near 14 degrees in Princeton, summer highs reach about 85 in July, and August is the wettest month at roughly 4.8 inches, which a buyer's inspector may keep in mind when looking at a basement or a roof.

  • Census estimate for 2025: 32,510 residents, 2.3% below the 2020 base, with 24.9% aged 65 or older.
  • Housing: 15,663 units, a 76.1% ownership rate and a median owned-home value of $126,900.
  • Rent and income: median gross rent of $832 and median household income of $69,257.
  • Commuting: 21.1 minutes on average, and only 16 building permits were issued in 2025.

Which Bureau County offices do I deal with on property tax?

Two county offices work out of the courthouse at 700 South Main Street in Princeton, keeping weekday hours of eight to four. The treasurer, who doubles as county collector, prepares and collects bills. The Supervisor of Assessments supports the township assessors, processes exemptions, and serves as clerk to the Board of Review.

Bureau County tax offices (source: Bureau County website)
OfficeWherePhoneHandles
Treasurer and CollectorRoom 103815-872-3241Bills, payments, tax sale
Supervisor of AssessmentsSuite 12815-875-6478Exemptions, equalization, appeals clerk

The township assessor, elected locally, starts the process by finding and valuing property. If a bill reaches you for a house you no longer own, the treasurer asks that it be returned promptly.

How and when do I pay Bureau County property tax?

The county issues a single bill that is payable in two installments, and partial payments are refused. Illinois law treats an installment as late on the later of June 1 or the day after the date printed on the bill (35 ILCS 200/21-15), so the coupon on your own bill is the date to follow. Not getting a bill, or getting it late, does not excuse the tax or the late charge.

  • In the office, only a check or cash is accepted, with checks payable to "Bureau County Collector."
  • By mail to Bureau County Collector, 700 S. Main St., Room 103, Princeton, IL 61356. A postmark on the due date is acceptable.
  • Online by debit or credit card or e-check through Illinois ePAY, which is available only through the second installment due date.
  • If a mortgage company pays your bill, contacting that company is your responsibility.

A canceled check serves as your receipt, and the treasurer will send a separate one if you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

What does a late payment cost in Bureau County?

The treasurer's page sets out three charges. Interest runs at 1.5% per installment per month on payments made after the due date, and the late-payment schedule is printed on the installment coupons. A payment sent without the late fees is returned. A further $10.00 is added to any tax still unpaid after the second installment date, covering publication and the certified delinquent notice.

Once those notices are mailed, the collector takes only certified funds: a cashier's check, money order or cash. Personal and business checks are refused. At the end of each tax year the collector holds a sale of the tax on every parcel still unpaid. A seller who has fallen behind should clear the balance before listing, since an open delinquency will appear in the title search.

How does a Bureau County assessment appeal work?

Illinois assesses nonfarm property at 33 1/3% of fair market value, and the Bureau County Board of Review rules say the same. An owner who disagrees files an appeal form with the Board's clerk, the Supervisor of Assessments, by the thirtieth day after the township's assessment list is published. Filing costs nothing, and a separate form is needed for each parcel unless the parcels are contiguous and similarly classified.

The rules focus on market value or equity, and the amount of a tax bill is not a valid complaint. For a home, the Board looks for:

  • Proof of a recent sale or purchase of the property.
  • A recent appraisal from an Illinois certified appraiser, delivered within 30 calendar days after the filing deadline and prepared to professional standards.
  • At least three recent sales of comparable properties, or assessed values of comparables if equity is the issue.
  • Dated photographs when you claim a condition problem.

The Board sends a tentative notice and an unhappy owner has ten days to schedule a hearing. Hearings run in 15-minute slots in the Supervisor of Assessments' office. Owners may speak for themselves or hire an Illinois attorney, and a missed hearing can lead to dismissal. An incomplete form is returned once with ten more calendar days to fix it.

What should I know about exemptions before listing in Bureau County?

The Board of Review rules state that homestead exemptions are applied under state statute and Department of Revenue guidelines, and that the deadline to apply for any of them is December 31. The Supervisor of Assessments processes exemption, preferential assessment and abatement applications and applies them to eligible parcels.

Because exemptions depend on who owns and occupies the home, a buyer should expect to apply in their own name. A seller can ask the Supervisor of Assessments which exemptions are on the parcel and bring that list to the closing so credits are estimated on real numbers. The county website carries the Board's rules and appeal form, along with GIS imagery that shows parcel boundaries and aerial photos.

How are Bureau County taxes handled at closing?

Illinois bills a year behind, so the bill that arrives after a sale usually covers the period before it. The Adams County collector's guide describes a seller credit at closing for tax not yet billed, and a Bureau County contract can settle the same point in writing. For the payment status of the parcel, call the treasurer's office at 815-872-3241.

  • Confirm whether both installments for the prior bill are paid.
  • Agree in the contract how the next bill will be split.
  • Give the county the buyer's mailing address, so assessment notices and bills reach the right person.
  • Keep copies of the deed and transfer paperwork, since the Board of Review accepts a recent purchase as evidence of value.

More questions about Bureau County, IL Property Tax Guide

How many installments does Bureau County property tax have?

Two. One bill arrives and is payable in two installments, and the county refuses partial payments. The coupon on your bill shows each date.

Is there a fee to appeal a Bureau County assessment?

No. The Board of Review rules say there is no fee for filing an appeal. The deadline is the thirtieth day after your township's assessment list is published.

Can I pay Bureau County tax with a credit card?

Yes, online through Illinois ePAY by debit card, credit card or e-check, until the second installment due date. The treasurer's counter accepts only checks and cash.

What happens to Bureau County tax I do not pay?

Interest builds at 1.5% per installment per month, $10.00 is added after the second installment date, and the collector holds a tax sale on unpaid parcels at year end. After notices go out, only certified funds are taken.

Where do I file a homestead exemption in Bureau County?

With the Supervisor of Assessments, 700 South Main Street, Suite 12, Princeton, phone 815-875-6478. The Board of Review rules give December 31 as the deadline to apply.

  • Board of Review: three members appointed by the County Board after passing a state exam. They hear complaints, equalize values between townships and add omitted property to the rolls.
  • Treasurer and Collector: mails roughly 77,000 real estate bills a year and distributes the money to 125 taxing districts. The office number is 217-384-3743.
  • County Clerk: handles redemption of taxes after a tax sale and calculates the rates once every taxing body files its levy.

The Treasurer's office is inside the Scott M. Bennett Administrative Center at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana, the county seat. Mobile homes are billed separately, about 3,400 of them, and those bills fall due sixty days after mailing.

What does Champaign County look like on the map?

Champaign County covers about 998 square miles of flat glacial plain in east central Illinois, and its county seat is Urbana. Champaign is the largest city, and the two cities nearly surround the University of Illinois campus. Other sizeable places include Rantoul, Mahomet and Savoy, which the 2020 Census counted at 12,371, 9,434 and 8,857 residents.

The county was organized in 1833, and the Illinois Central Railroad and later the land-grant university drove its growth. I-57, I-72 and I-74 all cross it, and Amtrak stops in Champaign and Rantoul. The northern end lost jobs when Chanute Air Force Base closed in the 1990s. Corn and soybean fields dominate the rural townships, so a farmhouse sale and a campus-area duplex sale can look nothing alike on a tax bill.

How is a home assessed and billed in Champaign County?

Assessments start with township assessors, who value property on a January 1 snapshot and send their work to the Supervisor of Assessments by June 15. Property is assessed at one-third of market value. If a township's level drifts from that share, the Supervisor can apply a township multiplier, and those multipliers are published in newspapers and on the county website.

The Illinois Department of Revenue reviews the county's assessments, and for the latest cycle that review took place in February 2026. For the 2025 tax year, payable in 2026, the Treasurer's FAQ says assessments were final by July 25, 2025, Board of Review appeals were finished by February 6, 2026, and the state issued a multiplier of 1, meaning it found the work properly done.

The largest slice of a bill goes to school districts. Each taxing body votes its levy by December 31 and files it with the County Clerk, and state law restricts most levy increases to the growth in assessed value and the consumer price index. All bills for the 2025 year were mailed by May 1. A bill that never arrives is still the owner's responsibility, so phone the Treasurer's office for a second copy.

What are the payment dates and methods for Champaign County bills?

Bills are usually mailed in early May and are typically due in June and September. For the 2025 tax year the FAQ lists June 3 for the first installment and September 3 for the second, and a payment postmarked on the due date counts as on time. Look at the coupon on your own bill for the current year's dates.

Late payments carry interest of 1.5% a month, or any part of a month, under state law, and a late payment schedule is printed on each coupon. A payment returned for any reason is void, with a $30 charge plus statutory interest. Personal and business checks are accepted through September 30. From October 1 the office takes only cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks at the counter.

  • Pay at a participating local bank listed on the county website.
  • Mail a check payable to Champaign County Collector, with the coupon, to P.O. Box 4306, Springfield, IL 62708-4306.
  • Pay online or by phone at 217-834-8713 with a card or eCheck, using the property's PIN. The processing vendor charges a fee.
  • Pay in person at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana, from 8 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon, Monday through Friday, with a 24-hour drop box in the parking lot.

Where do you file a challenge to a Champaign County valuation?

You file a complaint with the Board of Review between July 1 and September 10. The board takes complaints and holds hearings in that window, and after September 10 its members research values and issue written decisions. Office hours are 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., Monday through Thursday, or by appointment.

The board also represents the county in any appeal that continues to the state Property Tax Appeal Board. Bring paper that supports your number, such as the closing statement from a recent purchase and sales of similar homes nearby.

Which exemptions lower a Champaign County bill?

Exemptions reduce the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied, so they shrink the bill without changing what the house is worth. The Assessment Office exemptions page lists these reductions:

  • General homestead: a $6,000 reduction for the owner's primary residence on January 1 of the assessment year (Section 15-175).
  • Senior citizens: a $5,000 reduction owners who turn 65 by the end of the assessment year (Section 15-177).
  • Senior assessment freeze: holds the assessed value at a base year, with a maximum household income of $75,000, and renews each year with proof of income (Section 15-172).
  • Persons with disabilities: a $2,000 reduction (Section 15-168).
  • Veterans with disabilities: a reduction scaled to the service-connected disability rating, up to the full assessed value at 70% or higher (Section 15-169).

Faxed or emailed forms are not accepted, so call the office to have one mailed. When ownership changes, ask the office whether the seller's exemption ends and what the buyer must file.

What follows a missed payment in Champaign County?

The taxes are sold, and the house stays with the owner. In October the Collector mails a delinquent notice by certified mail and publishes the owner's name and amount in the newspaper. Anything still unpaid after 4:30 p.m. on October 29 goes into the annual sale on October 30, where a tax buyer pays the taxes and takes a claim against the property.

After the sale the owner owes the amount sold plus interest at the rate set on sale day. About two weeks later the County Clerk, at 217-384-3722, can quote the redemption figure, and a Take Notice from the Clerk arrives within four months. Redemption is paid to the Clerk, who repays the buyer. State law generally allows 3 years from the sale date, with exceptions spelled out in 35 ILCS 200/21-350, and a buyer whose claim is not redeemed can ask the circuit court for a deed.

What should be checked on the tax bill before a Champaign County closing?

Read the closing statement, because the Treasurer's office tells buyers and sellers to check closing documents, the title company or the attorney to learn whether tax is owed. Depending on the closing date and the date the deed was recorded, the bill can be mailed to the previous owner, who must forward it to the new owner.

Ask the Treasurer for a duplicate bill by PIN if one is missing, and confirm whether either installment is still open. If taxes are behind, ask about the amount to clear before closing, since unpaid taxes head toward the October sale. Whatever remains open for the current year is a closing item to settle with the title company or attorney.

More questions about Champaign County, IL Property Tax Guide

Which office mails Champaign County tax bills?

The County Treasurer, who doubles as Collector, mails them, normally in early May. A missing bill is still the owner's problem, and the office at 217-384-3743 issues duplicates.

What is the Champaign County appeal window?

July 1 through September 10, filed with the Board of Review. Members research values after September 10 and then issue written decisions.

Are personal checks taken at the counter after September 30?

No. The last day for a personal or business check is September 30. From October 1 the office accepts cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks in person.

Does a tax sale mean I lose my house?

Not right away. What gets sold is the unpaid tax, and the owner can redeem it through the County Clerk with interest. A court deed enters the picture only after the redemption period passes unused.

How much is the general homestead exemption in Champaign County?

The Assessment Office lists a $6,000 reduction in equalized assessed value for an owner-occupied primary residence. Call 217-384-3760 to have the application mailed.

Coles County by the numbers

Which courthouse offices run Coles County property tax?

Two courthouse offices split the work: the Supervisor of Assessments with the Board of Review sets and reviews values, and the Collector/Treasurer bills and takes payment. Both sit in the Coles County Courthouse at 651 Jackson Ave in Charleston, with the Board of Review in Room 133 and the treasurer in Room 124.

  • Bills, payments and the delinquent list: Coles County Collector/Treasurer.
  • Online look-up: the county's property tax inquiry portal shows assessment and tax data by parcel.

What does a seller see in Coles County's numbers?

Coles County is a prairie county of about 508 square miles in east central Illinois, organized in 1830 from Clark and Edgar counties. Charleston is the seat and the home of Eastern Illinois University. Mattoon and Oakland are the other two cities, and Ashmore, Humboldt and Lerna are villages. Twelve townships cover the rest.

Workers spend 18.2 minutes getting to work on average, and 91.1% of adults aged 25 or more have finished high school.

What are the 2026 Coles County tax dates?

The county splits each year's tax into two equal installments. A mailed payment should be taken inside the post office to be hand stamped, because a drop in a street box does not guarantee the right postmark.

How can I pay a Coles County tax bill?

Bring the original bill to the treasurer's office, which takes cash, checks and most credit cards. A payment drop box sits at the south entrance of the courthouse, and a second one is at Mattoon City Hall. Mail goes to the Coles County Collector, 651 Jackson Ave., Room 124, Charleston, IL 61920.

The key dates list also shows October 7, 2026 as the last day for personal checks and card or e-check payments ahead of the sale.

How can a Coles County owner contest an assessment?

You appeal the assessed value, never the tax bill, and you start with the Board of Review. The board opens its session on the first Monday in June, and the 2026 filing deadline posted by the county is December 14, 2026. The county's complaint forms state that the deadline is 30 days after the Supervisor of Assessments publishes the assessments.

An informal call to the assessor early in the year can sometimes fix a clerical error without a hearing. A written complaint to the Board of Review is required before any later appeal to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, and taxes stay payable while that appeal is pending. The state board's number on the county page is 217-782-6076.

  • A recent purchase on the open market or a professional appraisal supports a claim that the value is too high.
  • A wrong lot or building measurement is another listed ground.
  • Comparable homes, property record cards, photographs and a transfer declaration make up the evidence package.

Once the tax bill arrives it is too late to contest that year's assessment, which is why a seller with a recent price drop should act before the deadline.

What happens when Coles County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid parcels appear on a delinquent list published in a newspaper, then go to the annual tax sale. Buyers register by the day shown on the key dates list, file a letter of intent and pay a $250 registration fee that is applied to purchases. New buyers also need a letter of credit from their bank.

A sale does not move the deed. It places the unpaid tax in a buyer's hands, and the owner can pay it back during a redemption period. Ask the Coles County treasurer or clerk for the redemption deadline and payoff figure on any sold parcel before you list or sign a contract.

Mobile homes follow a separate track. Bills are mailed between March and May for the calendar year and are due 60 days after mailing. Interest runs $25 per month, capped at $100. A buyer needs a Mobile Home Certification filed with the Secretary of State to get clear title, and the treasurer can issue it once taxes are paid.

What should a Coles County seller check first?

Start with the parcel's tax history and ask your title company how both installments will be handled at closing. Then look at deadlines and paperwork.

  • Pull the parcel record on the county portal and confirm the bill name and mailing address.
  • Ask the treasurer whether any installment shows penalty and what the payoff is on a given day.
  • Check whether an appeal is open, since the 2026 filing window runs to December 14.
  • Gather repair estimates and any appraisal, since both support an appeal and a price discussion.

A home needing repairs can go to a cash buyer as is, and a tax payoff is taken from the sale proceeds.

When is the Coles County property tax deadline?

The first installment of the 2026 cycle was due July 1 and the second September 1. The treasurer's key dates also list October 9 as the delinquent list date. A 1.5% penalty applies to payments postmarked after the due date.

Where do I file a Coles County assessment complaint?

File it with the Supervisor of Assessments office in the courthouse at 651 Jackson Ave, Charleston, during weekday office hours. The Board of Review meets in Room 133. The county posted December 14, 2026 as the filing deadline for the 2026 session.

Can I pay Coles County taxes by card?

Yes. The treasurer accepts most credit and debit cards in the office, by phone and online. The card company charges a convenience fee, and an online check costs $1.00.

What is the Coles County tax sale?

It is the yearly auction of unpaid real estate tax. The 2026 sale was set for October 23 at 11:30 a.m. Buyers pay a $250 registration fee, and owners keep a redemption period to pay the amount back.

Does an appeal lower my Coles County tax bill right away?

No. An appeal challenges the assessed value, and any change flows into a later bill. You must keep paying while a state Property Tax Appeal Board case is pending.

How big is Cook County, and who bills the property tax?

Cook County bills property tax through its Treasurer at 118 N. Clark Street in Chicago, and values property through the Assessor and the Board of Review. It is the most populous county in Illinois and the second most populous in the United States, with more than 40 percent of the state's residents.

The county was created on January 15, 1831 and reached its present boundaries in 1839, when DuPage County was carved out of it. Growth was fast: the 1840 census counted 10,201 people, and the county passed 2.4 million by 1910. Construction of the Illinois and Michigan Canal began in 1848, and the county shares Illinois's Lake Michigan shoreline with Lake County. Today the land is almost entirely developed, with little farmland left near the outer boundaries.

When were Cook County's recent installments due?

Which Cook County townships are reassessed in 2026?

The Assessor reassesses one part of the county each year on a three year cycle. In 2026 the south and west suburbs are reassessed and every owner there receives a Reassessment Notice with the property's characteristics and new estimated fair market value. The north suburbs and the City of Chicago are reassessed only when something changes, such as a permit or division work.

An owner may appeal to the Assessor's Office and, separately, to the Board of Review. The Assessor's calendar lists a notice date and a last file date for each township. A sample of the 2026 south and west schedule, as listed:

The Assessor's page also shows Board of Review appeal periods, which open after the roll is certified. Updated values appear online one business day after the mailing date, and by law the assessment roll must also be published in a print newspaper. Check your township on the calendar for the exact window.

How does the Cook County tax sale work?

The Treasurer holds an annual sale of delinquent taxes, and the sale now scheduled to begin December 15, 2026 covers delinquent tax year 2023 taxes and special assessments. It runs from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on each sale day. Townships are grouped by day: December 15 starts with Barrington, Berwyn, Bloom, Bremen, Calumet, Cicero, Elk Grove, Evanston and the other alphabetically early townships through Orland, and later days continue through Hyde Park, Jefferson, Lake, Lake View and the rest. A re-offer day follows on December 21.

The sale is online at the county's tax sale site, and final bids can only be placed from computers in the Treasurer's sale room at 118 N. Clark Street, Room 112. Buyers register between November 6 and December 4, 2026 and post collateral. Delinquency lists went on sale at $250 for the general tax list and $250 for the special assessment list.

Parcels are offered as is, and the PIN alone, not the street address, identifies the delinquent taxes. A homeowner can search any PIN on the Treasurer's website to see whether taxes are delinquent, and the site has a page titled "If Taxes Were Sold" for owners whose parcel was already sold.

What relief programs does the Cook County Treasurer list?

  • Senior citizen assessment freeze and the Senior Citizen Real Estate Tax Deferral Program.
  • Persons with disability, home improvement and disabled veteran exemptions.
  • Property tax relief for military personnel and a first responder surviving spouse abatement.
  • Certificate of Error and refund forms, including an overpayment refund search.

Ask the Treasurer which exemptions appear on your PIN, and read each program page for its own rules.

What should I do about Cook County taxes before selling?

Gather the PIN, the last two bills and the township name, then compare them with the Assessor's calendar to see whether an appeal window is open. Check the delinquent search, and if your parcel appears on a tax sale list, contact the Treasurer before signing a contract.

  • Record the deed with the County Clerk after closing.

Payments can be made online with a bank account or card, by mail or in person, at Chase Bank, or at local community banks. The Treasurer's office is at 118 N. Clark Street in Chicago.

Which DuPage County offices deal with property tax?

Four county offices share the job. The Supervisor of Assessments coordinates the nine township assessors and publishes assessment changes, the Board of Review hears appeals, the Treasurer bills and collects, and the County Clerk handles redemption after a tax sale.

  • Supervisor of Assessments: 630-407-5858, for exemptions and assessment questions.
  • Board of Review: 630-407-5888, for complaint hearings.
  • County Treasurer: bills, payment, the delinquent list and the annual sale.
  • County Clerk: 630-407-5500, for an estimate of redemption on sold taxes, and 630-407-5540 for a change of billing name or address.

Assessment questions start with the township assessor named on your tax bill. The nine townships are Wayne, Bloomingdale, Addison, Winfield, Milton, York, Naperville, Lisle and Downers Grove.

What should a seller know about DuPage County itself?

DuPage County sits directly west of Chicago and was cut out of Cook County on February 9, 1839. Wheaton is the county seat and Naperville is the largest city. The county covers about 327 square miles of land, crossed by the DuPage River and Salt Creek, and almost all of it is developed. Before Lake Michigan water arrived in the 1990s, shallow dolomite wells supplied up to 60% of the county's water.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page lists 934,298 residents in July 2025 and 370,517 housing units.

  • Owner occupied rate: 73.1% for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median value of an owner occupied home: $391,400.
  • Median household income: $112,096, and median gross rent: $1,688.
  • Median monthly owner costs: $2,450 with a mortgage and $1,056 without one.
  • Building permits in 2025: 1,265.

Mean commute is 27.7 minutes and 51.8% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

When do DuPage County property tax bills come due?

The county mails one bill a year with two coupons. For the 2025 taxes billed in 2026, mailing began April 29, the first installment was due June 1 and the second September 1. The Treasurer's page states that Illinois law adds 1.5% interest per month to a late installment, and the bill says a U.S. postmark decides whether a mailed payment is late.

Late taxes follow a set path toward the sale. Pre-delinquent bills went out September 28, and the payment deadline to stay off the newspaper list was October 2. The delinquent list was published the week of October 12, and certified delinquent bills were mailed October 21. From November 2 only cash, a cashier's check or a money order is accepted, and an extra $10 covers the publication and certified mailing. The last day to pay was November 18 by 4:30 p.m., and the sale for unpaid 2025 taxes began November 19.

The bill itself lists the parcel number (PIN), the township assessor, the tax code, the fair cash value and an equalized value that the county page describes as one third of fair cash value. Sellers should keep the PIN handy, since it identifies the property in every county office.

When is the appeal deadline in my DuPage County township?

Each township has its own deadline, set at 30 days after the township's assessments are published. The Supervisor of Assessments posts the dates on its Assessment Status page. For 2026 the final complaint dates were:

The Board of Review rules say the filing period is not extended while you talk with the township assessor, so file inside the window even if a conversation is still going.

How does a DuPage County assessment appeal work?

Starting in 2026 the Board of Review requires every appeal to be filed electronically through the county's SmartFile system, and anything sent outside the 30 day window is rejected. Call or visit the township assessor first to check your property record, then file if you still think the value is too high.

The county asks for three or more comparable properties. For a market value claim the comparables must be recent sales, and for a uniformity claim they should be similar homes with similar features. The county notes that assessed values rest on the three prior years of sales, so the 2025 value drew on sales from 2022, 2023 and 2024.

  • A recent appraisal or a recent sale of your own house is the best evidence.
  • Written decisions are mailed after all county hearings finish, usually the following March.
  • A decision can be appealed to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of the notice.

Behind the scenes, township assessors finish their entries by November 15 of the assessment year, the Supervisor of Assessments applies a township equalization factor where needed, and the state can add its own factor before the Clerk computes rates.

What exemptions can lower a DuPage County bill?

The Treasurer's page lists several. The residential exemption lowers the taxable value up to $8,000 for a home you lived in on or before January 1 of the tax year, and the township assessor initiates it. The senior citizens homestead exemption is also up to $8,000 and needs proof of age and ownership.

  • Senior assessment freeze: household income limit of $65,000, with an application.
  • Disabled persons exemption: an annual $2,000 reduction in assessed value.
  • Homestead improvement exemption: up to $25,000 of added assessment from improvements, continuing up to four years.
  • Disabled veterans and returning veterans: contact the Supervisor of Assessments at 630-407-5858.

Ask the township assessor how a new owner applies after closing.

What happens if DuPage County taxes are sold at the tax sale?

The Treasurer's sale is an auction of interest rates. Buyers bid the rate they will earn, the lowest rate wins, and the winner pays the unpaid tax on the owner's behalf. The legal maximum bid is 9%, and the Treasurer reports an average winning bid of 2% per six month period in November 2025. A buyer pays the tax, interest and $124.00 in costs per parcel, then holds a certificate of purchase that acts as a lien.

The owner keeps title during redemption. The County Clerk's redemption page gives a minimum of 2 1/2 years for residential property of one to six units and 2 years for other classes, which a buyer may extend to 3 years. After that the buyer can petition the circuit court for a tax deed.

If your taxes were sold, call the Clerk for an estimate of redemption and share it with your title company. The Treasurer states that the sale is not reported to credit agencies.

More questions about DuPage County, IL Property Tax Guide

When is the second installment due in DuPage County?

For the 2025 taxes billed in 2026 the second installment was due September 1. The first was due June 1. Illinois law adds 1.5% interest per month to a late installment.

Can I still appeal if my township's window has closed?

No. The window ends 30 days after the township's assessments are published, and late appeals are rejected. Next year's schedule appears on the Supervisor of Assessments' Assessment Status page.

How do I file a DuPage County assessment appeal?

File it electronically through the county's SmartFile system, which the Board of Review has required since 2026. Attach at least three comparable properties. Hearing decisions are mailed the following March.

What is the redemption period after the DuPage County tax sale?

It is at least 2 1/2 years for a residential property of one to six units and 2 years for other property. A buyer can stretch the final date to 3 years. Call the County Clerk at 630-407-5500 for an estimate.

Who do I call about a DuPage County exemption?

Call the Supervisor of Assessments at 630-407-5858 or your township assessor. The residential and senior exemptions are each up to $8,000, and the senior freeze has a $65,000 income limit.

Who bills and reviews property tax in Effingham County?

The Supervisor of Assessments sets up and defends assessments, the Board of Review hears complaints, and the County Treasurer mails the bills and takes the money as county collector. The County Clerk figures tax rates and runs the redemption process after a tax sale.

When are Effingham County property taxes due?

Effingham County bills in two installments, and the county's treasurer FAQ for 2025 taxes payable in 2026 lists September 25, 2026 and November 6, 2026. Both of those dates have passed. Each year's dates are set when the bills go out, so read the stubs on your own bill.

Illinois taxes are paid a year behind, which is why the county describes the cycle as two years long. In year one, each parcel receives a valuation tied to the first of January. In year two the county applies rates, mails bills and passes the money to the taxing districts. The 2025 bills were mailed on August 21, 2026, and the treasurer asks anyone who has not received one by September 11 to call. A bill that never arrives does not excuse the tax or the late penalty.

The county collects for more than 90 taxing districts, and it also bills drainage, mobile home and railroad taxes.

How do I pay an Effingham County tax bill?

You can pay by mail, in person, at a bank or online. Whichever route you choose, the county wants the original bill or one printed from its website, and a $1 copy fee applies to other paperwork.

  • By mail with the installment stub and a check, carrying a postmark no later than the due date
  • Walking in to the Treasurer's counter
  • At most banks in the county, but as long as the bill is not yet late, since banks cannot take past-due payments
  • Online by credit card or e-check, which adds a convenience fee and can take up to seven days to post

When a lender escrows your tax, phone the lender and ask if it wants a copy of the bill. A seller who no longer owns the property and does not owe the tax under the closing statement should forward the bill to the new owner.

What if an Effingham County tax installment goes unpaid?

Delinquent tax picks up a 1.5% monthly penalty, and the amount rises every 30 days. After the due date, only the Treasurer's office can take payment, by mail or online.

For the 2025 payable 2026 cycle, the county lists these later steps: certified delinquent notices mailed November 30, 2026 with a $10 per parcel fee, no personal or business checks after those notices, online payments accepted until December 27, 2026, and a tax sale on January 7, 2027 in the North room of the County Office Building. The county says the sale is of unpaid taxes and not of the property itself, and that a payer can still settle up to one business day before the sale.

The county has elected under Public Act 104-0553 to acquire all delinquent taxes as trustee for the taxing districts. After a sale, ask the County Clerk for an estimate of redemption. If a seller still owes delinquent tax, the title company must get the exact balance from the collector before closing.

How do I appeal an assessment in Effingham County?

The Board hears testimony on property claimed to be over-assessed or under-assessed, either confirming the value or correcting it. Hearings finish in early February. An owner who disagrees with the Board can go to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court. Read the board's yearly rules and filing information before you send anything in.

Which exemptions and payment plans does Effingham County offer?

Amounts are set by state law and change, so get current figures from that office.

The Treasurer also assists senior citizens who apply for the state real estate tax deferral and approves those who meet the rules.

An optional nine-month prepayment plan, called TREASURER 9, spreads next year's tax over monthly payments due on the 15th. It currently runs January through August, costs nothing, and requires no delinquent taxes. The sign-up deadline is October 15, and the payments follow the most recent tax amount for the parcel.

What should sellers know about the Effingham County market?

Effingham County is in south central Illinois, where the city of Effingham is both the seat of government and the biggest town. Fayette and Crawford counties gave up land to form it in 1831. It covers about 479 square miles of land across fifteen townships, and Interstate 70 crosses it. Altamont, Teutopolis, Mason, Watson, Dieterich and Beecher City are among the other communities.

The Census Bureau counts 34,519 residents in its 2025 estimate and 15,520 housing units. Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $189,500 for 2020 through 2024, and homeowners live in 78.2% of the units. Median household income is $80,404, median gross rent is $733 and the average commute is 18.1 minutes. The county issued 50 building permits in 2025.

Average temperatures in the county seat run from a January low near 18 degrees Fahrenheit to a July high near 87.

How are property taxes settled when an Effingham County house sells?

The seller and buyer negotiate the split, and the county tells anyone who bought in late 2025 or 2026 to check the closing papers or ask the closing agent whether tax is owed. Depending on recording dates, the bill may have been addressed to the previous owner.

A buyer should confirm the parcel number, a ten-digit index number printed at the left of the bill under the owner name. If a seller faces a tax sale or delinquent bill, the collector's office can quote the balance for the title company.

When is the second installment of Effingham County property tax due?

For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the second installment was due November 6, 2026 and the first was due September 25, 2026. Both have passed. Bills are mailed in late summer and show the exact dates on the stubs.

What does paying Effingham County taxes late cost?

Late tax costs 1.5% for each month, growing every 30 days. Once the due date passes, banks cannot take the payment, so it must go to the Treasurer's office by mail, in person or online.

Does Effingham County sell my house if I do not pay property tax?

No. The county tax sale is a sale of the unpaid tax, and a buyer pays the tax and then charges interest. You can still pay until one business day before the sale, or redeem afterward through the County Clerk.

Where does an Effingham County assessment appeal go?

Send it to the Board of Review inside 30 calendar days of the date your township's assessment changes are published. Get the parcel-specific form from the Supervisor of Assessments at 217-342-6711.

The County Clerk, at 217-342-8433, computes rates from each district's levy. The Supervisor of Assessments at 217-342-6711 answers equalized assessed value and exemption questions, and the Treasurer at 217-342-6844 handles bills and payments.

How is a Franklin County property tax bill calculated?

Two numbers drive it: the value your township assessor gives the property, and the money your local taxing districts say they need for the coming year. The assessment office compares the process to income tax, where a rate is applied to a base.

About 60% of the property tax collected goes to education, and the rest is shared among the county, cities, park districts, library districts, fire districts, townships and other special districts. The treasurer's page says money is spread across more than fifty local governments, and the largest share goes to the school district where the property sits.

Rates are part of the puzzle too. Assessments can fall while rates climb, because a rate depends on the total levy and the total equalized assessed value in the district. A rate report for 2025 taxes payable in 2026 is posted on the Treasurer's page, and your own bill shows the rate for your taxing districts.

Properties inside a tax increment finance district work differently. Taxes on growth above the "TIF Base" go to the TIF fund instead of the other taxing bodies. The Treasurer gives the formula as (Net Taxable Value minus TIF Base) times the Tax Rate, and notes that the county does not create TIF districts or control how the money is spent.

What are the late penalties and tax sale rules in Franklin County?

All evidence must go in with the original complaint, because the Board looks only at what it receives. An overvaluation complaint needs proof such as an appraisal. A complaint about unequal treatment needs five comparable properties in your area with square footage, age and condition for each.

If you are unhappy with the Board's ruling, the next stop is the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board. The Treasurer adds that a taxpayer who still has a dispute after the complaint process can go to circuit court, but must keep paying the billed tax meanwhile to avoid tax liens. Keep a copy of whatever you file as proof.

Which exemptions can Franklin County homeowners claim?

The dollar amounts change almost every year, so ask the assessment office for current figures. Only the general homestead and senior homestead exemptions skip annual renewal. Seniors can also use the county's real estate tax deferral through the Treasurer, which puts a lien on the home and is repaid when it sells or transfers, and the state's Circuit Breaker grant is applied for with the Illinois Department of Revenue.

What should sellers know about Franklin County itself?

Franklin County is in Southern Illinois, in the region called Little Egypt. The county holds 409 square miles of land plus a good deal of water, including the Wayne Fitzgerrell State Recreation Area.

Coal shaped the county. Mining began in 1889 at the King Coal Mine, and the county saw eleven mine disasters between 1905 and 1968. The Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925 struck West Frankfort and killed 192 people in the county.

Census QuickFacts counts 36,916 residents in 2025, down 2.3% from the 2020 base, and 18,461 housing units. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $89,000 for 2020 through 2024, 74.1% of housing units are owner-occupied, and median household income is $56,740. Median gross rent is $803 and 16.4% of residents live in poverty. Only 19 building permits were issued in 2025.

Public school districts include Benton Community Consolidated District 47, Christopher Unit District 99, Frankfort Community Unit District 168, Sesser-Valier Unit District 196, Zeigler-Royalton Unit District 188 and Ewing-Northern Community Consolidated District 115.

How do property taxes work when a Franklin County house sells?

The tax bill is mailed to the owner at the address on the deed. According to the Treasurer, in typical transactions the seller compensates the buyer for real estate taxes at closing, and the two sides negotiate that point between them.

Call the Treasurer for the installment dates and the amount still owed on the parcel, since the bill itself carries the exact figures. A house with unpaid taxes can be in line for the tax sale, so a seller who is behind should clear it up before the sale date. How fast can a Franklin County tax buyer charge interest?

A winning bidder at the tax sale charges the owner interest at an initial maximum rate of 18%. If the tax buyer pays later years' taxes too, the initial rate on those is 12%.

Who hears assessment complaints in Franklin County?

The Board of Review hears them. It has three citizen members appointed by the County Board, and complaints are due within 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published. Appeals from the Board go to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

What do the Census figures say about homes in Fulton County?

At those values, an unpaid tax bill or a long repair list takes a bigger bite out of a sale than it would where homes cost more.

How is a Fulton County tax bill figured?

The Treasurer's bill insert gives the formula: equalized assessed value (EAV), minus exemptions, times the total local tax rate equals the bill. The EAV is typically 33 1/3% of fair market value, adjusted by a state-mandated multiplier. The major taxing bodies are school districts, the county, municipalities, townships and special districts such as park, library, fire protection and sanitary districts.

The Treasurer's page describes the scale of the roll. For the 2023 levy payable in 2024, about 26,500 bills went out, the extension was over $55 million, and distributions went to 122 taxing bodies. Net taxable value for that roll was $640,830,290 after $98,623,839 of exemptions. Distributions to the taxing bodies are made every 30 days from the first due date.

Fulton County bills a year behind. Taxes on the 2024 assessment were mailed in 2025, with the first installment due June 13 and the second due September 5, per the Treasurer's report to the County Board. Both dates have passed. Each bill carries two payment stubs. Read the dates on the current bill, since the county says a bill that never arrived is still owed.

How and where can a Fulton County bill be paid?

The Treasurer takes payment in person, by mail, at most county banks, in a courthouse drop box, online and by phone. Cash, personal checks, cashier's checks, money orders and cards are accepted at the counter, and cards carry a convenience fee. Each channel stops working at a different point in the year, which matters for anyone paying after a closing date slips.

Fulton County payment channels and cutoffs (source: Fulton County Treasurer, Payment Options page)
ChannelWhat the county says
Courthouse counterMonday to Friday, 8:00 am to 4:00 pm; bring the stubs
MailMust be postmarked on time; a postage meter imprint is not accepted as proof

The county's 2025 bill insert adds that mail is postmarked when processed, not when dropped off, effective December 24, 2025, so a hand-stamp at a post office counter or an early mailing is safer. Returned checks carry a $25 fee.

What happens if a Fulton County bill is paid late?

Unpaid Fulton County tax carries 1.5% interest for each month or part of a month. The bill insert cites 35 ILCS 200/21-15 for that rate and notes that the payment scale on each stub shows the penalty for each date range. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-135 the collector also collects $10 for certified mailing, advertising and publication costs.

  • 35 ILCS 200/20-25 lets the collector refuse a personal or corporate check within 45 days before a tax sale.
  • Unpaid parcels are published and certified letters are mailed, then the Treasurer takes judgment from the circuit court and runs the delinquent tax sale.
  • The Treasurer's tax computation page lists those steps, along with the County Clerk's role in calculating rates and collecting redemptions on sold taxes.

Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure by parcel number before any closing. The county's online property tax inquiry searches by parcel number, owner name, address, sale price or tax code, and it prints the bill and the payment history for each parcel.

How does a Fulton County assessment appeal work?

An owner who disputes the value can ask the township assessor or the county deputy assessors for an informal review, then file a complaint with the Board of Review. The complaint window opens with the newspaper publication for the township and lasts 30 days, and that publication date moves every year. A tax bill itself cannot be appealed. Once it arrives, only errors of fact such as a missing exemption or wrong square footage can be fixed through the Assessment Office.

The Board of Review rules for assessment year 2025 add details that matter to people in the middle of a sale. The person filing must hold a legal interest at the time, and that includes a recorded deed, a recorded contract for deed or installment memorandum, or a purchase agreement fully signed by both parties. Complaints go in by hand or by mail, courier or parcel service, with a postmark on or before the last filing day. The Board does not accept email or fax.

  • Equity appeals compare assessments of similar nearby homes. Market value appeals rest on recent sales of comparable homes.
  • Evidence the county names: a realtor's market analysis, a certified appraisal, a comparable sheet, a closing statement and photographs.
  • After a tentative decision and a hearing, a final notice goes out. An owner still unhappy has 30 days from that notice's postmark to go to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

Which exemptions can lower a Fulton County bill?

Fulton County lists seven homestead exemptions, and the owner is responsible for applying for each one. The Assessment FAQ tells owners to check the bill every year to confirm they receive all they qualify for.

  • General Homestead Exemption for owner-occupied residences.
  • Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption for owners over 65.
  • Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Exemption, which holds the assessed value at a base year with income limits. The county stresses that it does not freeze the tax bill amount.
  • Homestead Improvement Exemption for added value from a new improvement on a parcel that also has the general exemption.
  • Returning Veteran's, Disabled Veteran's (at least 50% service-connected disability certified by the VA) and Disabled Persons' exemptions.

A new owner-occupant should ask the Assessment Office, extension 113, which filings are needed after the deed is recorded. A seller who moved out midyear can ask the same office how that year's exemption is handled.

What should a Fulton County seller do about unpaid or unclear tax?

Start with the parcel number, which is printed at the top left of the bill and is also searchable online. Pull the payment history, confirm which installments are open, and ask the Treasurer for the total owed with penalties through the expected closing date. Bring the Assessment Office any exemption that should be on the parcel, because an error of fact can be corrected after the bill is issued.

A house with deferred repairs, back taxes or an estate attached can sit on the market in a county where the median is this modest. Some owners choose a direct as-is sale to a cash buyer, which skips the repairs and puts the tax settlement into the contract. On any route, get the payoff in writing from the Treasurer.

More questions about Fulton County, IL Property Tax Guide

When are Fulton County property taxes due?

Two installments, with dates that move from year to year. The 2024 taxes payable in 2025 had June 13 and September 5 deadlines, and both are behind us. The stubs on the current bill carry the live dates, or call (309) 547-3041, extension 132.

Who sends the Fulton County tax bill?

The County Treasurer, who also serves as ex-officio County Collector, prints and mails the bills. Before that, the County Clerk works out the rates and the Assessor sets values and approves exemptions. If nothing arrives in the mail, call the Treasurer anyway.

What is the penalty for paying Fulton County taxes late?

Interest of 1.5% accrues for each month or part of a month. The county's bill insert cites 35 ILCS 200/21-15 for that rate and 35 ILCS 200/21-135 for a $10 mailing and publication charge, and each stub prints a scale of amounts by date range.

How long do Fulton County owners have to appeal an assessment?

Thirty days, counted from the newspaper publication for your township, and that date shifts yearly. File with the Supervisor of Assessments, who is the Board's clerk, by hand or postmarked mail, since email and fax are refused. The next level, the Property Tax Appeal Board, has its own 30 day clock from the final notice's postmark.

Can someone under contract to buy a Fulton County house file an assessment complaint?

Yes, if the purchase agreement for the property is fully signed by both parties. The Board of Review rules list a recorded deed, a recorded installment memorandum, a contract for deed or lease-to-own on file, and a fully executed purchase agreement as qualifying legal interest.
