Grundy County by the numbers

What is Grundy County and who collects its property tax?

Grundy County is part of the Chicago metropolitan area, and Morris serves as both the seat and the biggest city. It was set off from LaSalle County on February 17, 1841, and spans 430 square miles, 418 of them land. Coal mining drew the first wave of workers, and today the county is better known for the Dresden Generating Station and the Mazon Creek fossil beds, where Illinois's state fossil, the Tully Monster, was first found.

The Grundy County Treasurer, working as County Collector, sends and collects the bills from the courthouse at 111 E. Washington Street in Morris. The Supervisor of Assessments oversees values, administers exemptions and also acts as clerk to the Board of Review. The Supervisor of Assessments does not collect tax, calculate it or set the rate, so questions about the dollar amount on a bill go to the Treasurer and the taxing districts.

  • Seventeen townships: Aux Sable, Braceville, Erienna, Felix, Garfield, Goodfarm, Goose Lake, Greenfield, Highland, Maine, Mazon, Morris, Nettle Creek, Norman, Saratoga, Vienna and Wauponsee.
  • Villages include Braceville, Carbon Hill, Gardner, Kinsman, Mazon, South Wilmington and Verona, and parts of Channahon, Coal City, Dwight, Minooka and Seneca.
  • School districts include Coal City CUSD 1, Herscher CUSD 2, Morris Community High School District 101 and Minooka Community High School District 111.

How do Grundy County home prices compare with the rest of Illinois?

Grundy County is one of the faster-growing and higher-priced counties in this part of Illinois. By the July 2025 estimate, 54,052 people live here, 2.8% more than the 2020 base, in 21,652 housing units. Owners hold 74.4% of the occupied homes.

  • Owner-occupied home value, midpoint for 2020 to 2024: $271,700.
  • Monthly cost of owning with a mortgage: $2,016. Gross rent: $1,177.
  • Median household income: $92,235. Persons in poverty: 5.8%.
  • Permits pulled in 2025: 114. Commute: 26.8 minutes each way on average.

At a median value of $271,700, a late installment here carries a penalty that grows every month it sits. Sellers who inherited a house or fell behind on payments should find out the open balance early.

When are Grundy County property tax bills due?

Grundy County bills one year behind and sends bills in two installments. For the 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the Treasurer's page set mailing no later than May 22, a first installment due Friday, June 26, and a second due Friday, September 4. All of those dates have passed. Mobile home bills for that year were due Friday, August 28, 2026.

The schedule differs from one tax year to the next, so confirm the year you are closing in with the Treasurer's office.

Grundy County payment rules by date (source: Grundy County Treasurer)
Date or periodRule
Through October 15Electronic checks accepted
October 1 and laterCash, cashier's check, credit card or money order only; no personal or business checks; $10 publication fee added to delinquent parcels
Through October 31Major credit cards accepted
Any late payment1.5% penalty per month under Illinois law

Card payments carry a 2.5% convenience fee with a $3 minimum, and e-checks a $1.50 flat fee, both kept by the payment processor.

Where can a Grundy County tax payment be made?

The Treasurer takes payment online, by mail, by phone at 815-324-6390, in the drop box outside the Sheriff's Department, at participating banks and in person at the courthouse. The Treasurer's page lists OSB Community Bank, Grundy Bank, American Commercial Bank and Trust, Busey Bank, Morris Building and Loan, Old National, First Federal Savings, Midland, Heartland and Bank of Pontiac among the participating banks.

The county's Property Tax Inquiry Portal lets an owner or a buyer search a parcel, review the payment history, see the current amount due and pull up assessment data. Checking it before an offer is accepted shows whether either installment is open.

What happens to unpaid Grundy County taxes at the annual sale?

Unpaid taxes are sold at an annual tax sale held at the Grundy County Administration Building, 1320 Union Street in Morris. The sale for the 2024 taxes payable in 2025 took place November 4, 2025, at 9 am. Under Illinois Public Act 104-0553 and a standing direction of the County Board, the Treasurer will sell all legally eligible delinquent liens or certificates at future sales to Grundy County as Trustee for the taxing districts.

The Treasurer's notice explains that this acquisition transfers the tax lien or certificate, not immediate title to the house. If the taxes on a parcel were sold, the owner redeems by paying the unpaid tax plus fees at the County Clerk's office. A seller whose taxes went to sale needs the redemption amount from the County Clerk, given by parcel number, in hand before a closing is scheduled.

How do Grundy County assessment notices and appeals work?

The 2026 assessment notices carry a date of September 23, 2026 and the complaint deadline was Monday, October 26, 2026 at 4:30 pm. That window has closed. Complaints could be filed in person, by email to the Board of Review address, or by mail postmarked by 11:59 pm on the deadline day. The 2026 data feeds the tax bills mailed in 2027.

The Board of Review publishes the equalized assessed values in two newspapers, the Coal City Courant for Braceville, Felix, Garfield, Goodfarm, Goose Lake, Greenfield and Maine townships, and the Morris Herald-News for Aux Sable, Erienna, Highland, Mazon, Morris, Nettle Creek, Norman, Saratoga, Vienna and Wauponsee. A change starting with tax year 2026 is that a notice is not mailed when a parcel moved only by the equalization factor or state farmland values. Those owners check the online Assessment Inquiry using the parcel number without dashes.

  • The Board of Review assesses omitted property, hears written complaints, equalizes between property classes, hears exemption requests and issues certificates of error.
  • Forms and the 2026 rules and procedures sit on the Board of Review page of the county site.
  • Decisions can be taken to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board, and then to the courts.

Which relief programs does Grundy County list for homeowners?

The county's Property Tax Relief page describes the state programs and the form each one needs. Applications go to the chief county assessment office, except the deferral, which runs through the Treasurer.

  • General Homestead Exemption: for a principal residence, with a maximum $6,000 reduction in EAV.
  • Senior Citizens Homestead Exemption: $5,000 off EAV for owners 65 or older.
  • Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Exemption: form PTAX-340 each year, with a household income cap printed on the county page.
  • Disabled Persons Homestead Exemption: $2,000 off EAV. Returning Veterans: $5,000 off EAV.
  • Disabled Veterans Standard Exemption: $2,500 for 30% to 49% disability, $5,000 for 50% to 69%, and full exemption at 70% or more.
  • Homestead Improvement Exemption: up to $75,000 for four years after the improvement is occupied.

The deferral program for senior citizens covers owners aged 65 and up whose household income is below $55,000. Under it the state pays the tax, records a lien, and collects the money back with 6% annual interest once the house is sold or transferred. A sale therefore ends the deferral. The Assessment Office can state the current income limit for the freeze.

What should a Grundy County owner do before selling with tax due?

Look the parcel up in the Property Tax Inquiry Portal and note which installments show as paid. Then request a total through the target closing date from the Treasurer. A parcel with a deferral lien needs a recovery balance, and sold taxes need a redemption figure from the County Clerk.

Even with strong values, a house that needs repairs or carries a tax problem can stall. Selling as is to a cash buyer skips repair negotiations, and the open balance gets settled in the purchase contract. Keep every payoff figure in writing.

When is the second Grundy County property tax installment due?

Friday, September 4 for the 2025 taxes payable in 2026, which is now behind us. The first installment fell on Friday, June 26. The Treasurer's page carries the schedule for each new tax year.

Can I pay Grundy County property tax with a personal check in October?

No. On and after October 1 the Treasurer accepts only cash, a cashier's check, a credit card or a money order. E-checks stop after October 15 and cards after October 31, and a $10 publication fee is added to delinquent parcels.

What does the Grundy County tax sale transfer to the buyer?

It transfers a tax lien or certificate, not title to the house. The Treasurer's notice says the county, acting as Trustee for the taxing districts, buys eligible liens at future sales. The owner redeems by paying the unpaid tax and fees at the County Clerk's office.

Who handles Grundy County exemption applications?

The Supervisor of Assessments administers homestead and non-homestead exemptions. Organizations seeking a non-homestead exemption apply through the Board of Review. Forms are on the county's assessor forms page.

How much is the penalty for late Grundy County property tax?

It is 1.5% a month, a rate the Treasurer attributes to Illinois law. Delinquent parcels also pick up a $10 publication fee after October 1. The Treasurer can quote an exact payoff for your parcel and date.

Henry County by the numbers

Where is Henry County and who handles its property tax?

Henry County is a flat, mostly agricultural county in northwest Illinois, with Cambridge as the seat and Kewanee as the largest city. It was formed January 13, 1825 out of Fulton County and covers 826 square miles. About 86.7% of the land is farmed, and the county belongs to the Davenport-Moline-Rock Island metropolitan area. New England settlers founded Andover, Wethersfield, Geneseo, Morristown and La Grange, and Cambridge itself was laid out in 1843.

The Treasurer and the Assessment Office share the building at 307 W. Center Street in Cambridge. The County Clerk files the levies and extends the tax to each parcel, usually finishing in April, and then the Treasurer prints and mails the bills. The Board of Review is made up of three citizens named by the County Board chair, and the Chief County Assessor serves as its clerk.

  • Treasurer: 309-937-3576, open Monday through Friday from 8 am to 4:30 pm except holidays.
  • Assessment Office: 309-937-3570, open Monday through Friday from 8 am to 4:30 pm.
  • Cities: Colona, Galva, Geneseo and Kewanee. Villages include Alpha, Andover, Bishop Hill, Cambridge, Cleveland, Orion and Woodhull.
  • Interstates 80, 74 and 280 cross the county, along with US 6, 34 and 150.

What do Census numbers show for Henry County housing?

Henry County has an older, owner-heavy housing base. The Census Bureau estimates 48,095 people for July 2025, 2.4% below the 2020 base, with 22,199 housing units. Owners occupy 79.9% of homes, and 24.1% of residents are 65 or older.

  • Median value of owner-occupied housing (2020 to 2024): $151,600.
  • Median selected owner costs: $1,414 with a mortgage and $581 without one.
  • Median gross rent: $842. Median household income: $71,911.
  • Building permits in 2025: 18. Mean commute: 22.2 minutes.

The county includes twelve K-12 school districts, among them Kewanee CUSD 229, Geneseo CUSD 228, Cambridge CUSD 227, Galva CUSD 224 and Orion CUSD 223.

How big is the Henry County tax roll?

The Assessment Office is responsible for just over 31,000 parcels with a total assessed value of $1,535,199,680. The County Clerk reports 124 taxing districts, 23 drainage districts and 27 TIF districts that all draw on the same levy process. Districts file their requests on the last Tuesday in December, and the Clerk checks them against the Truth-in-Taxation law and statutory rate limits.

Property is valued as of January 1 each year. On new construction, the county quotes the statute that makes the January 1 owner liable on a proportionate basis for the added tax from the date the occupancy permit issued or the improvement became fit for use through December 31. A seller who finished an addition last year should ask the Assessment Office how that proration affects the next bill.

Henry County bills in two installments. For tax year 2025 payable 2026, the Treasurer posted June 10 and September 10, 2026, and both dates have passed. Ask the Treasurer for the dates that apply to the tax year you are closing in.

How can a Henry County bill be paid, and what does it cost?

Payment is accepted by card, e-check, mail, drop box, in person, through local banks and by automatic withdrawal. Cards cost 2.25% plus $1.50 per transaction and e-checks $2, both paid to the processor. Banks cannot take payment after the second due date. The courthouse drop box takes everything except cash.

Henry County payment programs and limits (source: Henry County Treasurer)
ProgramTerms printed by the county
Automatic withdrawal (ACH)Debits on the first and second due dates; form must arrive 10 business days before a due date
Pre-paymentsDecember 1 to April 1; must be current on prior taxes; up to the previous year's amount only
Pre-payment methodsNo online payments or credit cards
Local banksEight named banks accept bills with the full statement; not after the second due date

With pre-payments, a bill later shows the remaining balance or a refund owed on overages once bills are generated, but money paid in advance cannot be pulled back before then.

What happens to unpaid Henry County taxes?

Unpaid taxes become delinquent, and the Treasurer runs a sale of the unpaid taxes every year. Tax buyers, both professional and private, bid for the right to buy the delinquent amount, and the winner pays the outstanding tax. The owner does not lose the house right away. Owners have two and a half years to redeem, after which the buyer may grant an extension or petition the Circuit Court for a tax deed.

  • Original interest on a sold tax can run from 0% to 18% annually, plus court costs, certified mailing and other fees.
  • Redemption goes through the County Clerk. Bring the parcel number, because the amount owed depends on the day.
  • Redemption must be paid in full by cash, money order or bank cashier's check. Illinois law does not allow personal checks or credit cards for it.

An owner selling a house whose taxes were sold should ask the Clerk for the redemption figure early, since the amount owed depends on the day.

What are the Henry County assessment and appeal dates?

The Chief County Assessor equalizes values and publishes changes between October 15 and November 15 of each year. The Board of Review accepts appeals for 30 days after publication, and an owner unhappy with the Board's written decision has 30 days from the date of that notice to go to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board. Splits and combinations of parcels must be requested by September 30.

Ask the Assessment Office for the Board of Review complaint form. The Board determines whether the township assessor and county assessor calculated values correctly. It can equalize assessments, add omitted property, decide on homestead exemptions and review non-homestead exemption applications.

  • The senior freeze income limit rose from $65,000 to $75,000. An owner with income at or under $75,000 who has never qualified can file the form on the county site or call the office.
  • Freeze forms for 2026 were mailed in January 2026 to everyone who qualified in 2025.
  • Ask the Assessment Office for the residential exemption applications.

What should a Henry County seller do about tax due at closing?

Open the county's Property Tax Inquiry site with the parcel number and read the bill and payment status. Phone the Treasurer at 309-937-3576 for a figure through the planned closing date, and call the Clerk if any year was sold at the delinquent sale. Ask the Treasurer which installments are still open for the year of closing.

With a countywide median value of $151,600, an old tax debt or a repair bill is a heavy share of what many Henry County houses are worth. Selling as is to a cash buyer is one way to avoid fixing the house and to settle the tax in the purchase contract, as long as the payoffs are confirmed in writing first.

More questions about Henry County, IL Property Tax Guide

When are Henry County property taxes due?

In two installments. For tax year 2025 payable 2026 they were due June 10 and September 10, 2026, and both dates have passed. The Treasurer posts the dates for each year on the Treasurer page of the county site.

Can a Henry County bank take my property tax after the second due date?

No. The county states that banks cannot accept payments after the second due date. After that the Treasurer's office is the place to pay, and a delinquent bill can go to the annual sale.

How long can a Henry County owner redeem sold taxes?

Two and a half years. After that the tax buyer may extend the time or petition the Circuit Court for a tax deed. Redemption goes through the County Clerk in cash, money order or cashier's check only.

How long do I have to appeal a Henry County assessment?

Thirty days after the assessments are published, which happens between October 15 and November 15. A further appeal to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board must be filed within 30 days of the Board of Review's written decision.

Does Henry County offer a way to pay property tax early?

Yes, a pre-payment program runs from December 1 to April 1. The payer must be current on prior-year taxes and may pay up to the previous year's amount only. A form is filled out each year at the time of payment.

Which offices deal with property tax in Iroquois County?

Two offices in the Iroquois County Administrative Center at 1001 East Grant Street in Watseka share the work. Room 105 is the Treasurer, who bills the tax and takes payment, phone (815) 432-6985. The Assessment Office, in Room 106, handles values, exemptions and appeals at (815) 432-6978. Both are open weekdays and close at half past four.

A three-member Board of Review sits apart from the assessor's staff and decides assessment complaints on the evidence shown at hearing. Township assessors in the county's townships handle first-line questions about a parcel's record.

  • Bills, payments and tax sale questions: the County Treasurer.
  • Exemptions, property record cards and address changes: the Assessment Office, where deputy clerks answer record requests by email.
  • Assessment complaints: the Board of Review, using the county's complaint form.
  • Tax rates: the County Clerk's Office.

What should a Watseka-area seller know about Iroquois County?

Iroquois County lies along the Indiana line in northeast Illinois, with its northern edge about 60 miles south of Chicago. It was cut from Vermilion County in 1833, and Watseka, the county seat since 1865, is also the largest city. Gilman is the other city. The county covers 1,117 square miles of land, which ranks third in Illinois, with Kankakee County to the north, Vermilion to the south and Ford to the west.

Interstate 57 runs along the western side past Chebanse, Clifton, Ashkum, Gilman, Onarga, Buckley and Loda, and U.S. Route 24 crosses the county from Gilman through Watseka to Sheldon. With 26 townships, the assessor for a parcel depends on its location, so check the township printed on the bill.

QuickFacts, the Census Bureau's profile page, shows an estimated 26,150 residents as of July 2025, compared with 27,077 counted in 2020.

  • Housing units: 12,780, with 80.0 percent of occupied homes owned by the people living in them.
  • Middle-of-the-range value of a home that its owner lives in: $137,800 for 2020 to 2024, against a median gross rent of $799.
  • Median household income: $66,255, and a mean commute of 25.0 minutes.
  • Only 14 building permits were recorded for 2025.

Nearly a quarter of residents, 24.9 percent, are 65 or older, so many owners here are thinking about downsizing or settling an estate.

When do Iroquois County tax bills come due?

The two installment dates are announced each year when bills are mailed, and they have moved around. The county's news releases give a first date in June in one year and in August in another. The dates on your own bill govern. A late balance picks up 1 1/2 percent for every month it sits unpaid.

Installment dates in two Iroquois County Treasurer news releases
Bills mailed forFirst installmentSecond installment
2021 taxes, payable 2022June 9September 9
2022 taxes, payable 2023August 18September 18

Bills carry two years, such as 2022 taxes payable 2023, so each bill is paid the year after its tax year. Request a written statement from the treasurer that lists every year still owing, and pass it to your title company.

Members of a United States Armed Forces Reserve unit called to active duty outside the continental United States may defer an installment until 180 days after returning, according to the same releases.

Where and how are Iroquois County bills paid?

You can pay at the treasurer's office in Room 105, by mail, at a participating bank or online through the county's property tax search page. The online route asks for the parcel number without dashes, the owner name or the address, then a Pay Taxes button appears.

  • Card payments online carry a charge of 2.35 percent plus $1.50, and e-check payments carry $2.00.
  • Banks that collect taxes include 1st Trust and Savings Bank in Watseka and Clifton, Iroquois Federal, Iroquois Farmers State Bank, Prospect Bank, First State Bank of Forrest and Commonwealth Credit Union, among others on the treasurer's list.
  • A drop box near the 911 Center at the Administrative Center accepts payments after hours.
  • Send or bring the whole bill. The county's releases say a $1.00 fee applies to payments made without it, and a receipt requires the full bill, with a stamped envelope if mailed.

The county's 2023 release adds that mortgage companies must make their payments online. When a lender escrows your tax, confirm which year it paid before ordering a payoff.

What is the route for contesting an Iroquois County assessment?

Complaints go to the Board of Review within 30 days of your township's assessment publication. Each township's cutoff is posted on the board's web page, according to its 2026 rules, and talking with a township assessor does not stop the clock.

The board's yearly session opens by the first Monday of June and continues day to day as needed. A reduction applies to the current assessment year only, except for omitted property. File all your evidence with the complaint itself, since the rules do not allow it to be added afterward.

  • Strong exhibits are an appraisal, comparable sales, the settlement statement from a recent purchase and current photographs.
  • A lawyer licensed in Illinois must file for property held by an LLC, partnership or corporation.
  • A party unhappy with the written decision has 30 calendar days to go to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, or may object in circuit court under 35 ILCS 200/23-5.

The assessment office adds that the board may adjust a value up as well as down, that reassessment happens every four years and that the target is one-third of fair cash value.

Which exemptions reduce an Iroquois County bill?

The general homestead exemption removes up to $6,000 from the equalized assessed value of an owner-occupied home before tax is figured, under 35 ILCS 200/15-175. The county's 2026 application asks for a state driver's license or ID showing the home address, and after first approval the exemption renews automatically. If the home stops being your main residence, you must have the exemption taken off.

The Board of Review rules list the other homestead exemptions administered through the county:

  • Returning veterans, disabled persons and disabled veterans (sections 15-167 to 15-169).
  • Senior citizens over 65 (section 15-170) and the senior assessment freeze (section 15-172).
  • The homestead improvements exemption (section 15-180).

To keep the bill correct, applications should reach the assessment office before the assessment year ends on December 31. The low-income senior freeze has its own filing window, January 1 through July 1. The treasurer also publicizes a senior property tax deferral program that works as a loan with interest, repaid when the property is sold or after the owner's death. Ask for current terms, since any deferral comes due at a sale.

What if Iroquois County taxes are not paid?

The treasurer's page carries tax sale buyer information and a buyer registration form, because unpaid parcels can be sold to a tax buyer at the annual sale. Buyers of tax certificates do not take your house at the sale. They gain a lien position and the right to petition for a deed if the owner never redeems.

Under 35 ILCS 200/21-350, redemption stays open for 3 years after the sale for certificates issued from January 1, 2024 onward, subject to exceptions that start with vacant property. Redemption payments go to the county clerk. The Iroquois County Clerk can give the exact deadline and payoff for a parcel that was sold.

What should be in order before an Iroquois County sale?

County records and your closing date need to line up, so start with the paper trail.

  • Get the parcel record and compare the owner name and mailing address against your deed.
  • Collect the treasurer's payoff figure for each year with an unpaid balance.
  • Learn which exemption should be dropped from the parcel after the sale.
  • See whether the Board of Review has an open complaint on your parcel.
  • Gather repair quotes if the house will be sold in its present state.

An as-is cash purchase is possible for an Iroquois County house, with any unpaid tax cleared in the settlement.

More questions about Iroquois County, IL Property Tax Guide

What are the Iroquois County installment dates?

The dates change each year and are printed on the bill. Past treasurer releases listed June 9 and September 9 for one year and August 18 and September 18 for another, with a 1 1/2 percent monthly penalty after each date.

Where can Iroquois County taxes be paid?

Options are the treasurer's counter at 1001 East Grant Street in Watseka, the mail, a participating county bank, the online property tax search page and the after-hours drop box.

How long is the Iroquois County appeal window?

Thirty days from publication of the township's assessments. Each township's date is posted on the Board of Review page, and talking with the assessor does not extend it.

What does the Iroquois County general homestead exemption remove?

Up to $6,000 comes off the equalized assessed value under 35 ILCS 200/15-175. File through the Assessment Office, Room 106, with a license or ID that shows the home address.

Which Iroquois County phone number answers tax questions?

Use (815) 432-6985 for the Treasurer and (815) 432-6978 for the Assessment Office. Rates are a County Clerk matter.

Jackson County by the numbers

Which offices run property tax in Jackson County?

Three Murphysboro offices share Jackson County's property tax work. The Treasurer collects, in the courthouse at 1001 Walnut Street, with a weekday schedule that ends at four, phone 618-687-7350. The Chief County Assessment Officer's staff and the Board of Review sit at 900 Walnut Street, at 618-687-7220 and 618-687-7226.

The treasurer's page is blunt about what that office cannot do: it has no authority to set the amount of a bill, change it or alter a mailing address.

  • Questions about an assessment: the township assessor or the Chief County Assessment Officer.
  • Missing exemptions and address changes: the assessment office.
  • Disputes over value: the Board of Review.
  • Prior-year back taxes that were sold: the County Clerk at 618-687-7360.

The county's Property Tax Lookup lets you search any parcel and print a bill, which is handy when a bill never arrived. Under state law the tax stays owed even if a bill is not received.

What does a Jackson County seller need to know about the area?

Jackson County sits in the Little Egypt region of southern Illinois, about 98 miles southeast of St. Louis. It was organized on January 10, 1816, with Brownsville as its first seat, and Murphysboro took over after the courthouse burned in 1843. Its biggest city is Carbondale, where Southern Illinois University has its main campus. The land area is about 584 square miles. Murphysboro, Carbondale, Ava and Grand Tower are the cities, and the March 18, 1925 Tri-State Tornado struck Murphysboro, Gorham and De Soto hard.

The July 2025 population estimate in Census QuickFacts is 52,501, against 52,974 counted in 2020, and the county has 27,715 housing units.

  • Owner households account for half of occupied homes, and renters for the rest.
  • The middle owner-occupied value is $137,300 (2020 to 2024), with rent at a median of $782.
  • Median household income is $48,763, and the poverty rate is 20.5 percent.
  • The county recorded 4 building permits in 2025, and 36.3 percent of adults 25 and older have a four-year degree or more.

If you own a rental house, ask the assessment office what the parcel record shows before you list it.

What did the 2026 Jackson County tax calendar set?

The treasurer's calendar for 2025 taxes payable in 2026 set the first installment at September 4, 2026 and the second at November 4, 2026. Partial payments are accepted through January 21. After an installment's due date, 1 1/2 percent accrues for every month or fraction of a month.

Once the sale has happened, late taxes are paid at the County Clerk's Office. Mobile home bills fall due every July 1, with a state-mandated late charge of $25 a month, capped at $100.

Where can a Jackson County bill be paid?

Jackson County takes payments online, by phone, by mail, at banks and at the counter. Online card or e-check payments go through Municipay, and the phone line for card payments is 618-492-4566. The courthouse drop box is at the top of the accessible ramp on the Chestnut Street side, for checks or certified funds only.

  • By mail: Jackson County Treasurer, P.O. Box 430, Murphysboro, IL 62966-0430.
  • At a bank: most Jackson County banks take payments on or before each installment date, but they will not take mobile home payments.
  • Convenience charges: cards cost 2.5 percent, never less than $2.00, and an e-check costs $1.
  • Prepaying: the treasurer lets you make estimated monthly payments toward the next bill free of interest.

Your parcel number (PIN) is on the Property Tax Inquiry page, or a call to the treasurer will supply it.

Which Jackson County districts receive the tax money?

The county's explanatory page shows how a recent tax year (2024 taxes payable 2025) was split among the districts. Schools take most of it.

  • All schools: 63.69 percent.
  • County purposes: 19.01 percent.
  • Cities, villages and incorporated towns: 7.37 percent.
  • Townships and road districts: 4.75 percent, and park districts 2.39 percent.
  • Airport, fire protection, conservancy, library and other districts share the remaining fraction.

Assessed value is meant to be 33 1/3 percent of market value, apart from farmland and farm buildings. The 2025 assessment notice put the required level at 33.33 percent and the countywide median level at 29.08 percent, with Carbondale at 30.85 percent, Murphysboro at 29.86 percent and Makanda at 26.50 percent. Each district's levy and any exemptions then set the dollars, so two houses of similar value can receive different bills.

What is the Jackson County appeal path?

Appeals go to the Board of Review within 30 days after the Supervisor of Assessments publishes a township's values. For 2026 the publication was set for October 29 and the deadline for the end of day on November 30, 2026. That window has closed, and the board's FAQ says no extensions are possible.

The board looks at value alone. A high bill, a steep percentage increase or a neighbor's smaller bill does not qualify by itself. Overvaluation, equity, physical data errors and preferential assessment are the four recognized reasons.

  • Each parcel needs its own form plus evidence, for example a recent appraisal, a settlement statement from the past two years or a comparison grid.
  • Owners or their attorneys file. Partnerships, LLCs and corporations must use an Illinois attorney.
  • Hearings are generally held by teleconference or phone, and failing to attend can get an appeal dismissed.
  • If you reject the proposed decision, you have 10 days to request a hearing, then 30 days from the final decision to go to the Property Tax Appeal Board.

When a hearing is set after a due date, the county advises paying what is due and taking any refund later. After those steps, a taxpayer who still objects pays under protest and files a tax objection complaint with the Circuit Clerk. A certificate of error corrects factual mistakes, like wrong square footage, but only on the current bill and before the annual tax sale.

What follows when Jackson County taxes are left unpaid?

First comes a certified letter, then newspaper publication of the unpaid parcel, then the annual sale of the tax. Buyers bid an interest rate between 0 and 9 percent. The sale auctions the unpaid tax, not the house.

The county's explanation puts the point at which a tax buyer can petition for a deed at 30 months without redemption. Section 21-350 of the statute sets 3 years for certificates issued from January 1, 2024, so the County Clerk can say which period fits your parcel. If no buyer bids, the tax goes to the Jackson County Trustee, and a deed the Trustee obtains goes to an annual sealed bid auction where the buyer is not responsible for the back taxes. The treasurer's page notes the last day to bid on the 2025 surplus auction was November 15, 2025.

Redemption of prior-year taxes is handled by the County Clerk at 618-687-7360.

What should a Jackson County owner check before listing?

A short checklist helps before you take an offer.

  • Print the tax history from the lookup page and see which installments were paid.
  • Ask the treasurer for a payoff when a penalty is accruing or a tax sale date is near.
  • Ask the assessment office how to remove your owner-occupied exemption once you move.
  • Ask the Board of Review whether an appeal on the parcel is still pending.
  • Photograph the defects a buyer may price in.

A Jackson County house can be sold as is for cash, and any tax balance is settled at closing.

For 2025 taxes payable 2026, the treasurer listed September 4 and November 4, 2026. A 1 1/2 percent penalty applies for each month or part of a month after an installment date.

Where does the Jackson County Treasurer work?

In the courthouse at 1001 Walnut Street, Murphysboro, on weekdays until 4. The phone number is 618-687-7350.

When did the 2026 Jackson County appeal window close?

Publication was set for October 29, 2026 and the filing deadline for the end of day on November 30, 2026. The board does not grant extensions.

What does paying Jackson County taxes online cost?

The treasurer's page links to Municipay. Cards add 2.5 percent, never less than $2.00, and e-checks add $1.

Who processes redemption of back taxes in Jackson County?

The County Clerk, 618-687-7360, who can quote the redemption amount and deadline for a given parcel.

Where is Jefferson County and which offices handle its property tax?

Jefferson County is in southern Illinois, in the area locals call Little Egypt, and Mt. Vernon is the seat, the county's settlers organized it on March 26, 1819, and it holds 571 square miles of land. Interstates 57 and 64 and U.S. 51 run through it, and its western edge touches the St. Louis commuter region.

A seller will deal mostly with two courthouse desks. The Treasurer/Collector sits at 100 South 10th Street, Room 100, Mt. Vernon, and answers at 618-244-8010 and keeps weekday hours that end at 4 p.m. The Assessor, whose formal title is Supervisor of Assessments, is in the same building at 618-244-8016. That desk doubles as clerk to the Board of Review, which puts appeals and exemption forms in one place.

The treasurer's page lists what it cannot do, which makes a handy call guide:

  • Mailing address changes on a bill, and every homestead, disability or senior freeze exemption: Assessor.
  • Complaints about how large the bill is: the taxing districts listed on the bill itself.
  • Redeeming delinquent tax: County Clerk, 618-244-8020.
  • Making or checking a payment: Treasurer/Collector.

How common is homeownership in Jefferson County?

Census QuickFacts counts 36,147 residents for July 2025, about 2.6 percent fewer than at the 2020 count. Of the 14,820 households, 71.7 percent own their home, and the typical owner-occupied house was valued at $126,000 in the latest five-year survey, and the median household brings in $63,118.

Against a house worth $126,000, a delinquent bill or a roof repair can take a real share of a seller's equity. Monthly housing costs for owner households come to $1,278 with a mortgage and $578 without. If your tax bill is behind and you want to skip listing prep, selling as-is for cash is one option to weigh against a traditional listing.

How does Jefferson County bill and collect real estate tax?

The county bills a year behind and posts a calendar on its Treasurer page. Tax for the 2025 assessment year is payable in 2026, and the statute lets an installment go delinquent after the later of June 1 or the due date printed on the bill, then adds interest at 1 1/2 percent for each month, or fraction of one, in a county this size (interest section of the Property Tax Code). A postmark on the due date itself still counts as on time.

Jefferson County dates for 2025 real estate tax payable in 2026 (source: Jefferson County Treasurer/Collector)

First installment dueAugust 28, 2026
Second installment dueSeptember 28, 2026

Annual tax sale auctionNovember 20, 2026

Mobile home tax runs on its own track: the page lists May 22, 2026 as that year's due date. The dates move from one cycle to the next, so request the calendar for the year your closing falls in.

How can I pay Jefferson County property tax?

Several payment routes exist, each with a catch. Make checks out to the Jefferson County Collector.

  • Online, by scanning the QR code on the bill. E-checks are free; cards are charged 2.25% or a $2.00 minimum, as the page prints it.
  • Most local banks, but only through the due date, and the payment stub must come along.
  • U.S. Mail, postmarked no later than the installment date, with the stub.
  • At the Treasurer's counter in the courthouse, which takes cash, check or money order and nothing else.

A personal check should arrive at least 45 days ahead of the tax sale so it can clear. When a lender escrows your tax, you still have to pass the bill along to that lender. Owners can also enroll in paperless billing or autopay on the county's payment site.

The county also takes optional prepayments for roughly six months once the second installment has passed, up to 100 percent of the last bill, provided no earlier year is delinquent.

What changed about the Jefferson County tax sale?

Two changes affect anyone carrying unpaid tax. The Treasurer's tax auction page says that, starting with the 2025 tax payable in 2026, the county chose, under Public Act 104-0553, to take over delinquent real estate taxes itself and hold them for the taxing districts. It also says the county adopted the Single Bidder Rule effective January 2026. Private buyers still bid on delinquent mobile home taxes.

Foreclosed parcels go to a separate sealed bid auction, and bids can be placed online at iltaxsale.com. Under state law, property sold at a tax sale can generally be redeemed within 3 years of the sale date, with exceptions tied to the property's condition on that date (redemption section of the Property Tax Code).

Mobile homes have an extra step. Taxes must be paid up to date before the home is moved or sold, and a tax certification from the Treasurer's office, costing $5, is filed with the Illinois Secretary of State to clear the title. Earlier unpaid years must be settled before the county takes current-year payment.

How can I challenge my Jefferson County assessment value?

Put the complaint in writing and send it to the Board of Review, which the Assessor's office administers. The county posted April 6, 2026 as the deadline for 2025 assessments, and that window has closed. State law sets the general clock at 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (complaint section of the Property Tax Code), so watch the newspaper notice each year.

Three appointed members sit on the Board of Review. If you disagree with its written decision, the Property Tax Appeal Board takes appeals filed 30 days from that notice (appeal board section of the Property Tax Code). Assessments outside Cook County are set at 33 1/3 percent of fair cash value (valuation section of the Property Tax Code), and the published notice gives a median level you can use to test your own figure.

Which exemptions can a Jefferson County homeowner use?

Below are the common homestead reductions from the Assessor's exemption page, with dollar figures exactly as the county prints them. Each lowers equalized assessed value, not the bill itself.

  • General homestead: any increase over the 1977 value, capped at $6,000, for an owner-occupant.
  • Senior citizen homestead: $5,000 once an owner reaches 65.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income of $65,000 or less for the 2025 application, with a new state law raising the limit in later years.
  • Homestead improvement: added value to a maximum of $75,000 a year for four years after completion.
  • Persons with disabilities: $2,000. Returning veterans: $5,000 for two years.
  • Veterans with disabilities: $2,500 for a 30 to under 50 percent rating, $5,000 for 50 to under 70 percent, and the first $250,000 of value at 70 percent or above.

The senior deferral program behaves like a loan: up to $7,500 of tax a year is deferred at 3 percent simple interest, repayable when the home sells or the owner dies, with applications taken January 1 through March 1. Anyone in this program should get the payoff total from the Treasurer before listing.

What should a Jefferson County seller handle before closing?

Print the parcel record from jeffersonil.devnetwedge.com, the county's inquiry site for bills and payments. Give the title company your parcel number plus the address the county mails to. If you have moved out, send the Assessor a change of address so later bills reach the right person.

Then find out whether an installment is open, whether a deferral lien exists and whether a lender escrows the tax. Have your title company explain how this year's tax gets divided at closing, and say in the contract who covers the bill that comes later. If a bill is already delinquent, get the interest-inclusive total from the Treasurer, and ask the County Clerk about any sold tax.

More questions about Jefferson County, IL Property Tax Guide

What dates appear on a Jefferson County tax calendar?

The county calendar for taxes payable in 2026 lists August 28 and September 28 as the two installment dates. Go by the date on your own bill, and since the calendar changes by year, request the cycle that matches your closing.

Who handles exemptions in Jefferson County?

The Assessor's office, at 618-244-8016, handles that. The Treasurer states that it cannot help with homestead, disability or senior freeze exemptions or with address changes on bills.

Can I pay Jefferson County tax with a card?

Yes, through the online payment site, where the county prints a charge of 2.25% or a $2.00 minimum. E-checks are free, and the courthouse counter accepts no cards.

What happens if Jefferson County tax stays unpaid?

The installment accrues interest after the due date, the parcel is published as delinquent, and the amount goes to the annual tax sale. After a sale, redemption goes through the County Clerk at 618-244-8020.

Must mobile home tax be current before I sell in Jefferson County?

Yes. The Treasurer requires mobile home taxes to be paid to date before a move or sale, and a $5 certification goes to the Illinois Secretary of State for a clear title.

What kind of place is Jersey County, Illinois, for a home seller?

Jersey County is a river county north of St. Louis, bounded by the Mississippi on the south, the Illinois River on the west and Macoupin Creek to the northwest. It was formed from Greene County on February 28, 1839, and Jerseyville is its seat and largest community. The Romanesque Revival courthouse there, finished in limestone cut at Grafton, had its cornerstone laid on July 4, 1893.

The county spans 369 square miles on dry ground and lies inside the St. Louis metro area. Many residents commute out of the county, and Census QuickFacts shows an average commute of 27.1 minutes. Roads include U.S. 67 and Illinois routes 3, 16, 100, 109, 111 and 267. Pere Marquette State Park near Grafton and Principia College near Elsah anchor the river end of the county.

Most of the county sits in Jersey Community Unit School District 100, with smaller parts in Southwestern District 9, Alton District 11 and Greenfield District 10. Look up your parcel number first, because township, school district and floodplain status all follow the parcel.

How many Jersey County households own their homes?

The Census Bureau estimates 21,160 residents for July 2025, down 1.7 percent from the 2020 base. Of the 7,965 households, 80.5 percent are owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $171,900. Median household income is $80,361, and the county issued 39 building permits in 2025.

Roughly one resident in four, 24.2 percent, is 65 or older. That matters for tax relief, since the Assessor's office helps seniors prepare the senior homestead exemption and assessment freeze applications.

Which Jersey County offices handle property tax?

The Treasurer, the Supervisor of Assessments, the Board of Review and the Code Administrator all work from the Government Building at 200 North Lafayette in Jerseyville, and all post the same weekday schedule, 8 to 4 The County Clerk answers rate questions and receives redeemed tax.

The Assessor's page also lists township assessors: one serves Jersey, Fidelity and Ruyle townships together, and another serves Mississippi Township. Since township assessors get the first look at an assessment, call yours before you file anything.

How is Jersey County real estate tax billed and paid?

The Treasurer's page says real estate tax is always a year behind when billed, while mobile home tax is for the current year. Due dates differ from year to year, so ask the office for the calendar covering your closing date. Interest is charged on anything paid after a due date, and state law sets that interest at 1 1/2 percent for each month, or fraction of one, in counties of this size (interest section of the Property Tax Code).

You have these ways to pay:

  • Online at jerseycountytax.com, where transaction fees apply.
  • Any of five Jerseyville banks, up to the due date only: Farmers State Bank, Heartland Bank & Trust, Jersey State Bank, Jerseyville Banking Center and Royal Banks.
  • The Treasurer's office or by mail once a bill is delinquent.
  • Mobile home tax, which can be paid only at the Treasurer's office or by mail.

A second property tax site, jerseyil.devnetwedge.com, is linked from the county pages for parcel inquiries.

What happens at the Jersey County tax sale?

The sale takes place in the auditorium of the Government Building. Only the delinquent taxes are sold, not the property itself. Once taxes are sold they must be redeemed through the County Clerk's office. If the taxes stay delinquent for 3 years, the Treasurer's page says the tax buyer can petition the court for a tax deed, and the redemption law carries exceptions that depend on the property's status on the sale date (redemption section of the Property Tax Code).

Before you list, ask the County Clerk for a redemption figure before you list, since sold tax has to be redeemed there.

How do I contest an assessment in Jersey County?

Begin with your township assessor, who has the first chance to change a value. If you cannot agree, ask the Board of Review for a hearing. The Board has three appointed members and hears complaints on value or exempt status for homes, businesses, condominiums and vacant land. It does not control the tax dollar amount, and a complaint about the bill itself is not a valid complaint.

A complaint must reach the Board no later than 30 calendar days after the newspaper prints the assessment list (complaint section of the Property Tax Code). For the 2025 changes, the county posted an appeal deadline of April 20, 2026, and that date has passed. Bring evidence to the hearing:

  • An exterior photo of your property and photos of at least three similar properties in your neighborhood.
  • Your property record card and the cards of comparable homes with lower assessments.
  • A recent appraisal, sales contract, settlement statement or deed, if you have one.

The Board mails its ruling. If you still disagree, the state Property Tax Appeal Board accepts a petition filed 30 days from the date of the decision notice (appeal board section of the Property Tax Code). The Assessor's forms page carries the Non-Farm Complaint (PTAX-230) and the Farm Complaint (PTAX-227).

Which exemption forms does the Jersey County Assessor offer?

The county's documents page lists applications by number, and the Assessor's office helps seniors prepare theirs. Ask the office for current dollar limits, because the county page names forms rather than amounts.

  • PTAX-329 and PTAX-340: senior citizens homestead exemption and assessment freeze, with separate 2025 and 2026 versions posted.
  • PTAX-343 and PTAX-343R: disabled person's homestead, initial and renewal.
  • PTAX-342 and PTAX-342R: standard homestead for disabled veterans.
  • PTAX-341: returning veterans.
  • PTAX-323: homestead improvement.
  • PTAX-245: disaster area reassessment.

For a house that was damaged, the disaster form may matter before you sell.

Do floodplain and permit rules affect selling a house in Jersey County?

They can. The Code Administration office reviews plans, issues building, storm water and floodplain permits, inspects new or substantially altered construction, and keeps elevation certificates for unincorporated Jersey County. It also keeps records of substantial improvements or damage to structures in the floodplain and investigates complaints under the International Property Maintenance Code.

Before listing a river-side or low-lying home, ask that office whether the parcel is in a mapped floodplain, whether any permit was left open, and whether a substantial-damage record exists. Manufactured homes fall under a county mobile home ordinance, and the Assessor's housing page links the state installation rules.

More questions about Jersey County, IL Property Tax Guide

When is Jersey County property tax due?

The county says due dates differ from year to year and that real estate tax is billed a year behind. Ask the Treasurer at (618) 498-5571 for the dates tied to your closing.

Where do I pay Jersey County property tax in person?

Real estate tax can be paid at five Jerseyville banks until the due date. After that, pay at the Treasurer's office in the Government Building at 200 North Lafayette, Suite 5.

Can I appeal my Jersey County assessment after the deadline?

The Board of Review handles complaints during a 30-day window after publication, so a missed window means waiting for the next assessment list. The posted date for the 2025 changes was April 20, 2026.

Does the Board of Review lower my tax bill?

No. It reviews assessed value only. The page says the tax dollar amount is not a valid complaint, and rate questions go to the County Clerk.

What is the fastest way to find out if my Jersey County parcel has tax sold?

Look up the parcel on the county's online tax site or call the Treasurer. If taxes were sold, redemption is made at the County Clerk's office.

What makes Jo Daviess County different for a home seller?

Jo Daviess County is the northwesternmost county in Illinois, with Galena as its seat. It sits in the Driftless Area, so the ground is steep and rugged compared with most of the state, and Charles Mound, the highest natural point in Illinois, is inside its borders. The county was formed in 1827, covers 601 square miles of land and is divided into 23 townships. Dubuque, Iowa and Platteville, Wisconsin are close by.

Its cities are Galena, East Dubuque and Stockton, and its villages include Apple River, Elizabeth, Hanover, Menominee, Nora, Scales Mound and Warren. Two census-designated places, Apple Canyon Lake and The Galena Territory, are also counted separately by the Census Bureau. U.S. 20 and Illinois routes 35, 78 and 84 are the main roads.

Census QuickFacts counts 21,594 residents for July 2025 and lists 13,535 housing units, but only 10,391 households for 2020 to 2024. That gap, together with the 2020 census count of 26.7 percent of units vacant, suggests a good deal of seasonal or second-home use. It matters at tax time, because homestead relief goes only to full-time resident owners.

What do the numbers say about owning a home in Jo Daviess County?

The Census Bureau puts the median value of owner-occupied homes for 2020 to 2024 at $209,900, with an owner-occupied rate of 80.4 percent. Median household income is $73,993. Residents 65 and older make up 31.5 percent of the population, and the 2020 census median age was 50.1 years.

An older owner base means plenty of estate and downsizing sales. If you are handling a parent's house, the exemption and deferral records in the next sections are worth pulling before a buyer's title search finds them.

Which Jo Daviess County offices touch a sale?

Both main offices are in the County Courthouse at 330 North Bench Street, Galena, and both keep weekday hours from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed on holidays.

The Assessment Office keeps the property record card for each parcel, tracks current owners from deeds filed with the recorder, and mails a notice to any owner whose assessment changed. Call it before your parcel is listed if you are unsure which township group covers the address.

How does Jo Daviess County collect real estate tax?

The Treasurer, who is also the County Collector, bills for roughly 110 local taxing bodies. After the Treasurer mails the bills, tax is payable in two installments, and any tax left unpaid at the end of the year is offered for sale after publication and notice. State law puts interest on a late installment at 1 1/2 percent for each month, or fraction of one, in counties of this size (interest section of the Property Tax Code).

The county site offers a free parcel search where you can reprint a bill, and an online payment system through Govtech Services. That system also lets an owner set up an individual escrow or advance payment for real estate tax. The Treasurer's forms page lists a deferral application, a direct deposit form and tax sale buyer registration forms. It also carries hotel and motel use tax returns, so anyone selling a lodging property should ask whether those returns are current.

Ask the Treasurer for the installment dates tied to your bill.

What are the property tax rates in Jo Daviess County?

The Assessment Office reports that tax rates in the county generally range from about 6.4554% to 11.21326%, with a median rate of 8.01228%. It adds that rates come from your taxing bodies, not from the Assessment Office. Where your parcel falls inside that range depends on the school, village, park and other districts it sits in.

The same page reminds owners that a homestead exemption reduces taxable value before tax is calculated, so the savings depend on the parcel's own rate. Check the district list on your bill when comparing two houses.

How do I appeal an assessment in Jo Daviess County?

Complaints go to the Board of Review, which has three appointed members and convenes on or before the first Monday in June. A complaint must be in writing on the prescribed form with original signatures, and the Board does not accept faxes. State law gives 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (complaint section of the Property Tax Code).

The 2026 cycle has closed. The county's notice says the final filing date for the 2026 assessment (payable 2027) passed for every township, that the Board may not take later complaints, and that the next chance is for the 2027 assessment (payable 2028), after notices are published in a local newspaper. The 2026 lists ran in The Galena Gazette for Council Hill, Dunleith, East Galena, Elizabeth, Guilford, Hanover, Menominee, Rawlins, Rice, Scales Mound, Vinegar Hill, West Galena and Woodbine townships. The Scoop carried Apple River, Berreman, Derinda, Nora, Pleasant Valley, Rush, Stockton, Thompson, Wards Grove and Warren townships.

After the Board rules, the Property Tax Appeal Board takes appeals filed within 30 days of the written notice (appeal board section of the Property Tax Code). Outside Cook County, the base is 33 1/3 percent of fair cash value (valuation section of the Property Tax Code).

Which exemptions apply in Jo Daviess County, and what is the residency rule?

The Assessment Office administers these homestead programs:

  • General homestead and homestead improvement.
  • Senior citizen homestead and senior citizen assessment freeze (PTAX-340).
  • Disabled persons (PTAX-343), disabled veterans (PTAX-342) and returning veterans (PTAX-341).
  • Disabled veteran standard exemption.

To qualify, you must be a full-time county resident and show two of three documents when asked: an Illinois driver's license, a federal tax return or an Illinois voter registration card, each listing the property address. Failing to produce two of three means disqualification from any homestead exemption. The county also warns that once bills have been printed, a missing renewal form for the low-income senior freeze, disabled person or disabled veteran exemption costs you that exemption for the year, with no exceptions.

Two other programs matter for an old house. The Treasurer's office handles the Senior Citizen Real Estate Tax Deferral Program, with applications available after January 1. And the Historic Freeze can hold the assessed value of an owner-occupied historic home for eight years, followed by a four-year step-up, but only after the state historic preservation office approves the rehabilitation. The county applies the freeze only after it receives that office's certificate.

What should a Jo Daviess County seller check before closing?

Work through this list before the contract is signed:

  • Pull the parcel from the county's free property search and compare it with your last bill.
  • Confirm which township group assesses the parcel.
  • Find out whether a deferral lien, a historic freeze or an exemption renewal is pending.
  • If a lender escrows your tax, ask it for the year's payment history.
  • Tell the title company about any lodging or short-term rental activity, since hotel and motel returns are filed with the Treasurer.

Your contract should say who pays the tax bill that arrives after closing and how the year is split, so that a buyer's first bill is not a surprise.

More questions about Jo Daviess County, IL Property Tax Guide

Is Jo Daviess County property tax paid in two parts?

Yes. The Treasurer states that real estate tax is payable in two installments after the bills are mailed. Ask the office for the dates printed on your bill.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Jo Daviess County assessment?

No. The county says the 2026 filing deadline has passed in every township and the Board of Review cannot accept later complaints. The next chance is the 2027 assessment, payable 2028.

What proof of residency does Jo Daviess County require for exemptions?

Two of three documents: an Illinois driver's license, a federal tax return or an Illinois voter registration card, each showing the property address.

Who do I call about my Jo Daviess County assessment?

Call the township assessor for the township where the home sits, or the county Assessment Office at 815-777-1016.

Does Jo Daviess County offer a tax deferral for seniors?

Yes. The Treasurer reviews and grants deferrals, and the application is available from that office after January 1 each year. Call 815-777-0355.

Where is Johnson County, Illinois, and who lives there?

Johnson County lies in the far southern part of Illinois, the region known as Little Egypt, with Vienna serving as seat and biggest city. It was organized in 1812 out of Randolph County and has 344 square miles of land. Williamson, Saline, Pope, Massac, Pulaski and Union counties surround it.

The 2020 census counted 13,308 residents, and every one of them was classed as living in a rural area. The state archives page notes that the county dropped township government in 1876, so its subdivisions are precincts: Bloomfield, Burnside, Cache, Elvira, Goreville, Grantsburg, Simpson, Tunnel Hill and Vienna. The Vienna Correctional Center, a state prison for men, skewed the county's 2000 census age profile toward male residents.

In Vienna, January lows average about 25 degrees and July highs reach about 90. Rain falls every month, and May is the wettest at roughly 5.2 inches, so check the roof, gutters and crawl space before a buyer's inspector does.

How many Johnson County homes are owner-occupied?

QuickFacts lists 13,363 residents as of July 2025 and about 5,555 housing units. Among 4,101 households for 2020 to 2024, 82.0 percent own their home. A typical owner-occupied house is worth $160,500, and households have a median income of $62,528.

Owner households pay a median $1,510 a month with a mortgage and $510 without. Median gross rent is $781, and the Census Bureau logged no building permits at all for 2025, so new construction is thin and most buyers will be looking at existing homes like yours. A clean title and paid tax bills make that sale simpler.

Which Johnson County offices answer property tax questions?

The County Clerk's site lists direct lines for the offices a seller needs. The Clerk and Recorder holds deed records back to 1815 and handles the recording of deeds and mortgages, plat books and delinquent taxes.

How are Johnson County tax bills searched and paid?

The county runs an online property tax inquiry portal at johnsonil.devnetwedge.com, with separate searches for parcels and for mobile homes, plus a link to pay taxes. Search by parcel number, owner name or street address and print the record for your title company.

The county's own installment dates should come from the Treasurer's office, because they change from year to year and appear on each bill. State law sets the penalty: an installment unpaid after the later of June 1 or the due date printed on the bill is delinquent and bears interest of 1 1/2 percent for each month, or fraction of one, in a county this size (interest section of the Property Tax Code). Mail postmarked by the deadline is not late. The second installment follows the same rule against the later of September 1 or the bill date.

Where a lender holds escrow and the tax goes delinquent through the lender's fault, the law puts the interest on the lender, so call the servicer first when a bill looks unpaid.

How does a Johnson County assessment work, and how do I contest it?

The assessment list is printed in a local newspaper by December 31 in a county this small, and the notice must give the median level of assessment, the filing deadline and a note on homestead exemptions (publication section of the Property Tax Code).

To test your figure, divide the assessed value by the median level in the notice. If the result is higher than what the house would sell for, you may be over-assessed. A complaint goes in writing to the Board of Review within 30 calendar days of publication, and a complaint filed by mail counts on its postmark date (complaint section of the Property Tax Code). If the Board's decision still looks wrong, the Property Tax Appeal Board takes a petition filed 30 days from the date of the written notice (appeal board section of the Property Tax Code).

Call the Assessor at 618-658-8010 to learn where the Board of Review takes complaints, which forms it wants and what board rules apply.

What homestead relief can a Johnson County owner claim?

The state code sets the amounts, and Johnson County falls in the group of counties that are not next to a county of 3,000,000 or more people. For 2023 and later years, that puts it in the lower tier of each exemption:

  • General homestead: the rise in equalized value above the 1977 figure, up to $6,000 (general homestead section).
  • Senior citizens homestead: up to $5,000 for an owner 65 or older who is liable for the taxes (senior homestead section).
  • Senior owners can also qualify to defer taxes, and the assessor must tell exemption holders so.

The same law keeps a homestead exemption alive through the end of the sale year in a county under 3,000,000, and the assessor may require the new owner to apply for the following year. A buyer should plan to file the paperwork early.

The Assessor can also tell you about disability, veteran and improvement exemptions, which have their own state forms. Ask which applications are due this cycle and whether a renewal is waiting.

What happens if Johnson County tax goes unpaid before a sale?

The County Clerk's office lists delinquent taxes among its services, and state law allows unpaid tax to be sold at a tax sale. Under state law, property sold at a tax sale can generally be redeemed within 3 years of the sale date, with exceptions that depend on the property's status on the sale date (redemption section of the Property Tax Code).

If your bill is behind, get a payoff figure with interest from the Treasurer, check with the Clerk on whether any tax was sold on the parcel, and give both numbers to the title company. Paying the balance at closing out of proceeds is common, but the contract should say so.

How should I prepare a Johnson County house for sale?

Start with the parcel record on the inquiry portal and confirm the owner name matches your deed.

  • Print the record and your last assessment notice for the buyer.
  • Pay or schedule the current installment, and ask your lender about escrow.
  • Call the Addressing line at 618-658-5911 if a rural parcel needs a corrected address.

If the deed is in a deceased relative's name, ask the Clerk and Recorder what is needed to record a transfer. If a manufactured home sits on the land, run the portal's separate mobile home search too.

Use the county's property tax inquiry portal at johnsonil.devnetwedge.com. It has separate searches for parcels and mobile homes, and a link to pay.

State law caps it at $6,000 of equalized assessed value for 2023 and later in counties that are not next to a county of 3,000,000 or more. The amount is the rise above the 1977 value, up to that cap.

Kane County by the numbers

How is Kane County laid out for a homeowner thinking of selling?

Kane County is a collar county of the Chicago area, with Geneva as the county seat and Aurora as its largest city. It was formed in 1836 out of LaSalle County and covers about 524 square miles, and its biggest cities (Aurora, Elgin, Batavia, St. Charles and Geneva) sit along the Fox River. The 2020 census counted 516,522 residents, which makes it the fifth most populous county in Illinois.

The county is a patchwork of cities, villages and townships, and that matters for a seller because the tax bill for one Kane County house can look very different from the bill for a house a few miles away. Elgin, Aurora, Batavia, Geneva, St. Charles, Carpentersville, Sugar Grove, Montgomery and Hampshire all have their own taxing bodies layered under the county. A Geneva address and a Hampshire address can pay different school districts and municipalities, even though one county treasurer sends both bills.

Which Kane County offices deal with property tax?

Four offices share the work in Kane County, and the Government Center campus in Geneva houses most of them. The county's own quick guide to property taxes sorts questions by office, so a seller can go straight to the right desk.

Kane County property tax offices (source: Kane County Quick Guide to Property Taxes, April 2025)
OfficeHandlesWhere and phone
Township Assessor (16 townships)Initial valuations, questions about your assessed valueDirectory at assessments.kanecountyil.gov
County Assessment OfficeExemptions, assessment complaints, equalization factors719 Batavia Avenue, Building C, Geneva, (630) 208-3818
County Clerk, Tax ExtensionTax rates, delinquent taxes, redemptions719 Batavia Avenue, Building B, Geneva, (630) 232-5964
County TreasurerCurrent tax bills and collection, forfeitures719 Batavia Avenue, Building A, Geneva, (630) 232-3565

Per the guide, phones are answered on weekdays, with county holidays off. Foreclosures go through the county sheriff, a point worth knowing if a sale is racing a lender.

How does Kane County assess a house?

A Kane County township assessor estimates the fair cash value of a home as of January 1 of the assessment year, and the assessed value is 33.33 percent of that figure. Assessors look at actual sales from the three prior years, and the county Supervisor of Assessments then equalizes values so townships line up with each other.

Kane County has 16 townships, and each one elects its own assessor: Aurora, Batavia, Big Rock, Blackberry, Campton, Dundee, Elgin, Geneva, Hampshire, Kaneville, Plato, Rutland, St. Charles, Sugar Grove, Virgil and Burlington. The valuation work happens at the township level, not at the county seat. Between general assessment years, assessors can still revise values after new construction, demolition, or fire and flood damage.

  • Farmland is valued on agricultural economic value, so a Kane County farm and a southern Illinois farm are valued the same way.
  • Preferential assessments exist for subdivision lots, historic residences, open space, low-income housing, veterans and fraternal posts, solar energy and railroads, each with its own conditions.
  • The county publishes that the tax cap law (PTELL) limits most local levy increases to 5 percent or inflation, whichever is less, with exceptions such as new construction and voter-approved referenda.

How do I appeal a Kane County assessment?

Talk to your township assessor first, then file a written complaint with the Kane County Board of Review within 30 days after your township's assessment notice is published in a local newspaper. The Board of Review is a three-member body that can raise, lower or confirm an assessment, and it also decides exemption requests.

Kane County recognizes three bases for a complaint. One is a physical data error, such as a record showing 2,400 square feet when a survey shows 2,200. Another is valuation, where the equalized assessed value is more than one third of fair cash value. The third is equity, where the assessment is higher than comparable homes nearby. The Property Tax Appeal Board has ruled that the dollar amount of the tax or the year-over-year percentage change is not a valid basis for an appeal.

Deadlines vary by township, and the county lists them on its Assessment Complaints page along with residential, commercial and association complaint forms and an electronic evidence portal. Once a tax bill arrives it is too late to complain for that year unless the complaint was already taken to the Board of Review. Subscribing to the assessment office's email notice tells you when your township's roll is published.

Which homestead exemptions does Kane County list?

The county's quick guide lists nine relief programs, and most reduce the taxable value rather than the bill itself. Applications are on the assessment office website or by phone at (630) 208-3818.

  • General Homestead Exemption, up to $8,000, for owner-occupied principal dwellings, usually without annual reapplication.
  • Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption, up to $8,000, once an owner turns 65 by the end of the assessment year.
  • Homestead Improvement Exemption, up to $25,000, on a new addition or finished basement for four years.
  • Low-Income Senior Citizen Assessment Freeze, with an annual application and a household income limit of $65,000 in the guide.
  • Returning Veterans' Exemption of $5,000 for two years after return from an armed conflict.
  • Standard Exemption for Veterans with Disabilities, up to $250,000, for a service-connected rating of at least 30 percent.
  • Veterans with Disabilities Exemption, up to $100,000, for Specially Adapted Housing.
  • Persons with Disabilities Exemption of $2,000.
  • Natural Disaster Exemption for reconstruction after a disaster.

Senior Services of Aurora and Senior Services of Elgin also help seniors apply.

When are Kane County property taxes due?

Kane County bills in two installments, and the 2025 taxes payable in 2026 were due June 1 and September 1, 2026. Bills were mailed on or before May 1, and the payment season for that tax year closed on Friday, October 23, 2026 at 4:30 p.m.

State law (35 ILCS 200/21-15) makes an unpaid installment delinquent after its due date and charges interest at 1 1/2 percent per month or portion of a month in counties of this size. Unpaid taxes can be offered at the annual tax sale. The county's guide says an owner whose taxes are sold can still redeem a principal dwelling for two and one half years, while other property must be redeemed within two years, paying costs and interest on top of the tax. Sold taxes are redeemed through the County Clerk's Tax Extension office, not the treasurer.

Payment options listed by the treasurer include online e-check (free), a drive-up drop box behind Building A, participating Kane County banks with a payment coupon, mail, the treasurer's counter, and the County Clerk's Aurora and Elgin branch offices for personal checks or money orders. A bill reprint is free online or $2.00 at the counter.

Who pays the tax when a Kane County house sells?

In Kane County the tax stays with the property, so a buyer can receive a bill for a year in which the seller lived there. The county tells new owners to read the closing statement for a credit from the seller or to ask their attorney.

The bill due in a given year covers the prior tax year, so a sale can land between a paid installment and an unpaid one. Your closing agent can show how the settlement statement splits the bill. The Treasurer can give the payment status of your parcel number (PIN), and the Clerk can give an estimate of redemption if a prior year went unpaid. A PIN appears on the bill and on the assessment notice, and the assessment office's Property Search tool will find it by address.

Where does Kane County property tax money go?

The largest share goes to schools, and the rest is split among municipalities, the county and other local governments. Kane County has no say in what other governments levy, since each taxing body sets its own levy and the county issues a levy only for itself.

By property type, the county reports that residential property supplies 75.7 percent of the tax base, commercial 12.8 percent, industrial 9.6 percent and farm 1.7 percent. The county's own extension rose from $58,345,127 for 2023 to $61,071,789 for 2024, an increase of 4.69 percent. Among school districts, the quick guide shows taxes billed for 2024 changing by 5.96 percent in Elgin 46, 3.10 percent in Geneva 304, 5.37 percent in Saint Charles 303 and a drop of 1.62 percent in Batavia 101. The guide gives tax rates generally between about 6 and 9 percent, with a median near 7.5 percent. A parcel lookup at the county's tax data site shows how much goes to each district for one property.

What does it cost to own a home in Kane County?

The Census Bureau estimates 525,757 residents for July 2025 and 195,957 housing units. Occupants own 76.0 percent of the homes, and the 2020 to 2024 survey puts a typical owned home at $327,000. Renters pay a median $1,453 in gross rent, and household income is $103,163 at the median.

Owners with a mortgage report $2,256 in monthly costs and those without one report $958. Builders pulled 1,629 permits in 2025. A seller facing back taxes or a delinquent notice should start with the treasurer and the clerk's tax extension office.

Which Kane County office sends the bill?

The Treasurer collects current taxes from Building A of the Government Center in Geneva, (630) 232-3565. For rates or redemption, call the Clerk's Tax Extension office at (630) 232-5964.

How long do Kane County owners have to file a complaint?

Thirty days, counted from the newspaper publication of your township's notice. The Board of Review takes the complaint, and publication dates differ by township.

Interest runs at 1 1/2 percent a month, and the taxes can be sold at the annual tax sale. A principal dwelling keeps a two and one half year redemption period, per the county's guide.

Yes, but the unpaid amount must be settled at closing or credited to the buyer, because the tax stays with the property. Ask the treasurer for the payoff and the clerk for a redemption estimate if taxes were sold.

Does Kane County offer a senior exemption?

Yes. The county guide lists a senior exemption of up to $8,000 and a separate assessment freeze that depends on household income.

Kankakee County by the numbers

How is Kankakee County laid out for someone selling a house?

Kankakee County lies south of Will County along the Kankakee River, with the city of Kankakee as both county seat and largest city. The Illinois legislature created it in February 1853 from the north part of Iroquois County and the south part of Will County, and it covers 681 square miles. It also borders Indiana to the northeast and east, with Lake County and Newton County across the line.

Only two cities sit in the county, Kankakee and Momence, so most Kankakee County homes are in villages, townships and rural areas. The county is divided into seventeen townships, and the county publishes a directory of township assessors. Most valuation work happens at the township level, so the number on a Kankakee County tax bill starts with a township valuation. The Census Bureau counted 107,502 residents in 2020 and estimates 105,525 for July 2025, a decline of 2.0 percent from the April 2020 estimates base.

Who runs property tax in Kankakee County?

Four bodies matter: the township assessor, the Supervisor of Assessments, the County Treasurer and the Board of Review. The Supervisor of Assessments and the Treasurer both work from 189 East Court Street in Kankakee, IL 60901.
